title: 2 Chronicles

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 1
summaryBullets: Now Solomon son of David established himself securely over his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and highly exalted him. (1:1).
Then Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every leader in all Israel— the heads of the families. (1:2).
And Solomon and the whole assembly went to the high place at Gibeon because it was the location of God’s Tent of Meeting, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness. (1:3).
Now David had brought the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it, because he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem. (1:4).
But the bronze altar made by Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, was in Gibeon before the tabernacle of the LORD. So Solomon and the assembly inquired of Him there. (1:5).
Solomon offered sacrifices there before the LORD on the bronze altar at the Tent of Meeting, where he offered a thousand burnt offerings. (1:6).
That night God appeared to Solomon and said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!” (1:7).
Solomon replied to God: “You have shown much loving devotion to my father David, and You have made me king in his place. (1:8).
Now, O LORD God, let Your promise to my father David be fulfilled. For You have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth. (1:9).
Now grant me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may lead this people. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?” (1:10).

God said to Solomon, “Since this was in your heart instead of requesting riches or wealth or honor for yourself or death for your enemies — and since you have not even requested long life but have asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern My people over whom I have made you king — (1:11).
therefore wisdom and knowledge have been granted to you. And I will also give you riches and wealth and honor unlike anything given to the kings before you or after you.” (1:12).
So Solomon went to Jerusalem from the high place in Gibeon, from before the Tent of Meeting, and he reigned over Israel. (1:13).
Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses, which he stationed in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem. (1:14).
The king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills. (1:15).
Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and Kue; the royal merchants purchased them from Kue. (1:16).

A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for a hundred and fifty. Likewise, they exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram. (1:17).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 3:4-15: The same night at Gibeon, where Solomon asks for a discerning heart and is given riches he did not ask for.
Exodus 31:1-11: Bezalel son of Uri is filled with the Spirit of God to make the tabernacle and its bronze altar.
Deuteronomy 17:16-17: The king must not multiply horses for himself or send to Egypt for them, or multiply wives, silver, and gold.
1 Kings 10:26-29: The same chariot force, with horses imported from Egypt and Kue and resold to the kings of the Hittites and Aram.
1 Chronicles 16:39-40: Zadok and the altar of burnt offering are left at the high place at Gibeon, where Solomon goes here.

translationNotes.note: What Solomon asks for in verses 10-12 is not private insight. Hokhmah covers practical skill of every kind: it is the word used of Bezalel's metalwork and weaving (Exodus 31:3-6) and of a sailor's seamanship (Psalm 107:27). Solomon asks for it in the specific form a ruler needs, to go out and come in before a people too many to number, which is a request for competence in judgment and administration.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד (ohel moed), tent of meeting
translationNotes.note: Verses 3-6 explain a split most readers miss. The tent Moses made in the wilderness, with Bezalel's bronze altar, still stood at Gibeon about six miles northwest of Jerusalem, while David had brought the ark into a separate tent in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:1,39). For a generation Israel had the altar in one town and the ark in another, which is why the new king goes to Gibeon to sacrifice.

A light two-wheeled platform pulled by a trained pair, carrying a driver and an archer. It was the most expensive weapon system of the age and needed level ground, a supply of horses, wheelwrights, and roads, which is why Israel's hill country had none for centuries while Egypt and Aram fielded thousands. Solomon's 1,400 chariots in verse 14 mark the moment Judah became that kind of power.

translationNotes.term: The price of a chariot and a horse
translationNotes.note: Verse 17 prices an imported chariot at 600 shekels of silver and a horse at 150. A shekel is a weight, about 0.4 ounces or 11.4 grams, not a coin. For scale, Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels as the compensation for a slave killed by an ox, and Judges 17:10 has a Levite hired for ten shekels a year with food and clothing. One chariot cost what twenty slaves were valued at.

Verses 16-17 have Solomon's merchants buying horses from Egypt and Kue and reselling them on to the Hittite and Aramean kings. Kue is the coastal plain of Cilicia in what is now southern Turkey, famous for its horse country. Judah sat on the land bridge between the two supply regions, so the crown ran the trade as a middleman and took the margin.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon establishes his kingdom with God's support, travels to Gibeon with Israel's leaders, and offers a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar; God appears to him that night and grants him wisdom and knowledge along with unprecedented wealth and honor because he did not ask for riches or long life. Solomon returns to Jerusalem and begins accumulating vast quantities of chariots, horses, silver, and gold, importing these goods from Egypt and selling them to neighboring kings.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 2
summaryBullets: Now Solomon purposed to build a house for the Name of the LORD and a royal palace for himself. (2:1).
So he conscripted 70,000 porters, 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains, and 3,600 supervisors. (2:2).
Then Solomon sent word to Hiram king of Tyre: “Do for me as you did for my father David when you sent him cedars to build himself a house to live in. (2:3).

Behold, I am about to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God to dedicate to Him for burning fragrant incense before Him, for displaying the showbread continuously, and for making burnt offerings every morning and evening as well as on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts of the LORD our God. This is ordained for Israel forever. (2:4).
The house that I am building will be great, for our God is greater than all gods. (2:5).

But who is able to build a house for Him, since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him? Who then am I, that I should build a house for Him, except as a place to burn sacrifices before Him? (2:6).

Send me, therefore, a craftsman skilled in engraving to work with gold and silver, with bronze and iron, and with purple, crimson, and blue yarn. He will work with my craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem, whom my father David provided. (2:7).
Send me also cedar, cypress, and algum logs from Lebanon, for I know that your servants have skill to cut timber there. And indeed, my servants will work with yours (2:8).
to prepare for me timber in abundance, because the temple I am building will be great and wonderful. (2:9).
I will pay your servants, the woodcutters, 20,000 cors of ground wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of olive oil.” (2:10).
Then Hiram king of Tyre wrote a letter in reply to Solomon: “Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king.” (2:11).

And Hiram added: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth! He has given King David a wise son with insight and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a royal palace for himself. (2:12).
So now I am sending you Huram-abi, a skillful man endowed with creativity. (2:13).

He is the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, and his father is a man of Tyre. He is skilled in work with gold and silver, bronze and iron, stone and wood, purple, blue, and crimson yarn, and fine linen. He is experienced in every kind of engraving and can execute any design that is given him. He will work with your craftsmen and with those of my lord, your father David. (2:14).
Now let my lord send to his servants the wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine he promised. (2:15).
We will cut logs from Lebanon, as many as you need, and we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa. Then you can take them up to Jerusalem.” (2:16).
Solomon numbered all the foreign men in the land of Israel following the census his father David had conducted, and there were found to be 153,600 in all. (2:17).
Solomon made 70,000 of them porters, 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains, and 3,600 supervisors. (2:18).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 5:1-18: The same agreement with Hiram of Tyre, the cedar and cypress from Lebanon, and the levy of workmen.
1 Kings 7:13-14: Huram the bronze worker, son of a widow of Naphtali and a man of Tyre, is brought to do all the bronze work.
Exodus 31:1-6: Bezalel and Oholiab are given skill in gold, silver, bronze, stonecutting, and carpentry for the sanctuary.
1 Kings 8:27: Heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain God, much less a house that Solomon has built.
2 Chronicles 8:7-10: The forced labour drawn from the peoples left in the land, with Israelites as the officers over it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חוּרָם אָבִי (Huram avi), Huram my father
translationNotes.note: Verses 13-14 send Solomon a master craftsman from Tyre whose mother came from the daughters of Dan and whose father was a Tyrian. The parallel at 1 Kings 7:13-14 calls his mother a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. Both stand as written. The suffix on his name is a title of respect for a master of a trade, and the skills listed, metal, stone, wood, dyed yarn, and engraving, are the whole range the temple needed.

Verses 17-18 count 153,600 foreign residents and put 70,000 to carrying, 80,000 to cutting stone in the hills, and 3,600 over them as supervisors. This is conscripted labour owed to the crown, not slavery bought and sold: men were called up in shifts for state building work. Resentment at the levy is what breaks the kingdom apart two chapters after Solomon dies, when the people stone the officer in charge of it.

Verse 16 describes how cedar reached Jerusalem. Logs were floated down the Lebanese coast lashed into rafts and landed at Joppa, the nearest usable harbour, about thirty-five miles from Jerusalem, then hauled inland and uphill by ox. Israel had no natural deep harbour of its own on that coast, and no cedar; both had to be bought from Tyre.

The largest biblical dry measure, about 58 gallons or 220 litres, equal to ten ephahs. Verse 10 promises Hiram's woodcutters 20,000 kors of wheat and 20,000 of barley, which is a food supply for a labour force rather than a payment in silver. The Greek form is the measure the debtor owes in the parable at Luke 16:7.

The liquid measure matching the ephah, about 5.8 gallons or 22 litres, used in verse 10 for the oil and wine. The bronze Sea in the temple court is rated in baths, and the two accounts give different capacities: 1 Kings 7:26 says two thousand baths, 2 Chronicles 4:5 says three thousand. Both figures stand in the text.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon conscripts tens of thousands of workers and sends Hiram king of Tyre a detailed request for cedar and a skilled craftsman; Hiram agrees to send Huram-Abi and timber in exchange for wheat, barley, wine, and olive oil.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 3
summaryBullets: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David. This was the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. (3:1).
Solomon began construction on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of his reign. (3:2).
The foundation that Solomon laid for the house of God was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, according to the old standard. (3:3).
The portico at the front, extending across the width of the temple, was twenty cubits long and twenty cubits high. He overlaid the inside with pure gold. (3:4).
He paneled the main room with cypress, which he overlaid with fine gold and decorated with palm trees and chains. (3:5).
He adorned the temple with precious stones for beauty, and its gold was from Parvaim. (3:6).
He overlaid its beams, thresholds, walls, and doors with gold, and he carved cherubim on the walls. (3:7).

Then he made the Most Holy Place; its length corresponded to the width of the temple— twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. And he overlaid the inside with six hundred talents of fine gold. (3:8).
The weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. He also overlaid the upper rooms with gold. (3:9).
In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of sculptured work, and he overlaid them with gold. (3:10).

The total wingspan of the cherubim was twenty cubits. One wing of the first cherub was five cubits long and touched the wall of the temple, and its other wing was five cubits long and touched the wing of the other cherub. (3:11).
The wing of the second cherub also measured five cubits and touched the wall of the temple, while its other wing measured five cubits and touched the wing of the first cherub. (3:12).
So the total wingspan of these cherubim was twenty cubits. They stood on their feet, facing the main room. (3:13).
He made the veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into it. (3:14).
In front of the temple he made two pillars, which together were thirty-five cubits high, each with a capital on top measuring five cubits. (3:15).
He made interwoven chains and put them on top of the pillars. He made a hundred pomegranates and fastened them into the chainwork. (3:16).
Then he set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south and one on the north. The pillar on the south he named Jachin, and the pillar on the north he named Boaz. (3:17).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 6:1-38: The same temple, dated to the four hundred and eightieth year after Israel came out of Egypt, with its measurements.
1 Chronicles 21:18-28: David buys Ornan's threshing floor and builds an altar there where the plague stopped.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is sent to the land of Moriah to offer his son, and a ram is provided instead.
Exodus 26:31-33: The veil of blue, purple, and crimson worked with cherubim, dividing the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
1 Kings 7:15-22: The two bronze pillars cast for the porch, one named Jachin and the other Boaz.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָכְמָה (ḥokhmah), Greek: σοφία (sophia), Aramaic: חָכְמְתָא (ḥokhməta)
translationNotes.note: Practical discernment in governance and justice; not mere knowledge but skillful application.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּבוֹד (kavod), Greek: δόξα (doxa), Aramaic: יְקָר (yeqar)
translationNotes.note: The manifest presence of God, filling the tabernacle and later the temple.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכָל (heikhal), Greek: ναός (naos), Aramaic: הֵיכְלָא (heikhla)
translationNotes.note: Palace/house of God; in Chronicles, the center of worship and covenant relationship.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

Verse 1 fixes the temple site on the ridge north of the City of David, on Ornan's threshing floor, and names it Moriah. That is the only other place the name appears outside Genesis 22:2, where Abraham is sent to the land of Moriah to offer Isaac. The chapter is placing the temple on ground already marked twice, by Abraham and by the stopped plague of 1 Chronicles 21.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָכִין (Yakhin), he establishes - בֹּעַז (Boaz), in him is strength
translationNotes.note: The two bronze pillars in verse 17 stood free at the porch and held nothing up; they were named, which no other part of the building was. Jachin means he will establish and Boaz means in him is strength. When Babylon took the temple apart, the pillars were broken up and carried away as bronze (2 Kings 25:13,16-17).

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon builds the temple foundation on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem and constructs its interior with extensive gold overlays, including the portico, main hall, Most Holy Place with gold-plated cherubim, a decorated curtain, and two pillars named Jakin and Boaz at the front entrance.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 4
summaryBullets: He made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high. (4:1).
He also made the Sea of cast metal. It was circular in shape, measuring ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits in height, and thirty cubits in circumference. (4:2).
Below the rim, figures of oxen encircled it, ten per cubit all the way around the Sea, cast in two rows as a part of the Sea. (4:3).
The Sea stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The Sea rested on them, with all their hindquarters toward the center. (4:4).
It was a handbreadth thick, and its rim was fashioned like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It could hold three thousand baths. (4:5).
He also made ten basins for washing and placed five on the south side and five on the north. The parts of the burnt offering were rinsed in them, but the priests used the Sea for washing. (4:6).
He made ten gold lampstands according to their specifications and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. (4:7).
Additionally, he made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. He also made a hundred gold bowls. (4:8).
He made the courtyard of the priests and the large court with its doors, and he overlaid the doors with bronze. (4:9).
He put the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner. (4:10).
Additionally, Huram made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. So Huram finished the work that he had undertaken for King Solomon in the house of God: (4:11).
the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars; the two sets of network covering both bowls of the capitals atop the pillars; (4:12).
the four hundred pomegranates for the two sets of network (two rows of pomegranates for each network covering both the bowl-shaped capitals atop the pillars); (4:13).
the stands; the basins on the stands; (4:14).
the Sea; the twelve oxen underneath the Sea; (4:15).
and the pots, shovels, meat forks, and all the other articles. All these objects that Huram-abi made for King Solomon for the house of the LORD were of polished bronze. (4:16).
The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zeredah. (4:17).
Solomon made all these articles in such great abundance that the weight of the bronze could not be determined. (4:18).
Solomon also made all the furnishings for the house of God: the golden altar; the tables on which was placed the Bread of the Presence; (4:19).
the lampstands of pure gold and their lamps, to burn in front of the inner sanctuary as prescribed; (4:20).
the flowers, lamps, and tongs of gold— of purest gold; (4:21).
the wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles, and censers of pure gold; and the gold doors of the temple: the inner doors to the Most Holy Place as well as the doors of the main hall. (4:22).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 7:23-39: The same bronze sea on twelve oxen, the ten stands and their basins, and the same casting in the Jordan plain.
Exodus 30:17-21: The bronze basin set between the tent and the altar, where Aaron and his sons wash their hands and feet.
Exodus 27:1-8: The bronze altar of the tabernacle, five cubits square and three high, with its horns and carrying poles.
Exodus 25:31-40: The lampstand of hammered gold with six branches and seven lamps, made after the pattern shown on the mountain.
2 Kings 16:17: Ahaz cuts the panels off the stands and takes the sea down from the bronze oxen onto a stone base.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָכְמָה (ḥokhmah), Greek: σοφία (sophia), Aramaic: חָכְמְתָא (ḥokhməta)
translationNotes.note: Practical discernment in governance and justice; not mere knowledge but skillful application.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּבוֹד (kavod), Greek: δόξα (doxa), Aramaic: יְקָר (yeqar)
translationNotes.note: The manifest presence of God, filling the tabernacle and later the temple.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכָל (heikhal), Greek: ναός (naos), Aramaic: הֵיכְלָא (heikhla)
translationNotes.note: Palace/house of God; in Chronicles, the center of worship and covenant relationship.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.
The width of four fingers, about 3 inches (7.5 cm). Used for small dimensions on temple furniture and as a metaphor for the brevity of life (Psalm 39:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָם מוּצָק (yam mutsaq), the cast sea
translationNotes.note: A single cast bronze basin, ten cubits across and five deep, about fifteen feet wide and seven and a half feet from brim to floor, standing on twelve bronze oxen in four groups of three facing out. Verse 6 says it was for the priests to wash in, the temple's replacement for the tabernacle's small bronze basin. At 2,000 baths, the figure given in 1 Kings 7:26, and about 5.8 gallons to a bath, that is over eleven thousand gallons of water weighing more than forty tons.

Verse 17 says the king cast the bronze work in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah. Bronze on this scale needed a place with the right casting clay for moulds, fuel, and room for furnaces, and it was done thirty-five miles from the building site, then hauled up. 1 Kings 7:47 says the bronze was never weighed because there was so much of it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hiram completes the bronze furnishings for the temple - a large altar, the Sea with twelve bulls underneath, ten basins, ten lampstands, and ten tables - and Solomon adds gold furnishings including the altar, lampstands, and doors. The total bronze work is so extensive that its weight cannot be calculated.

The Ten Basins, Lampstands, and Tables

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 5
summaryBullets: So all the work that Solomon had performed for the house of the LORD was completed. Then Solomon brought in the items his father David had dedicated— the silver, the gold, and all the furnishings— and he placed them in the treasuries of the house of God. (5:1).

At that time Solomon assembled in Jerusalem the elders of Israel— all the tribal heads and family leaders of the Israelites — to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Zion, the City of David. (5:2).
So all the men of Israel came together to the king at the feast in the seventh month. (5:3).
When all the elders of Israel had arrived, the Levites took up the ark, (5:4).
and they brought up the ark and the Tent of Meeting with all its sacred furnishings. The Levitical priests carried them up. (5:5).
There, before the ark, King Solomon and the whole congregation of Israel who had assembled with him sacrificed so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered. (5:6).
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim. (5:7).
For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and overshadowed the ark and its poles. (5:8).
The poles of the ark extended far enough that their ends were visible from in front of the inner sanctuary, but not from outside the Holy Place; and they are there to this day. (5:9).
There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, where the LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites after they had come out of Egypt. (5:10).
Now all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves regardless of their divisions. And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, (5:11).

all the Levitical singers — Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and relatives — stood on the east side of the altar, dressed in fine linen and playing cymbals, harps, and lyres, accompanied by 120 priests sounding trumpets. (5:12).

The trumpeters and singers joined together to praise and thank the LORD with one voice. They lifted up their voices, accompanied by trumpets, cymbals, and musical instruments, in praise to the LORD: “For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.” And the temple, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud (5:13).
so that the priests could not stand there to minister because of the cloud. For the glory of the LORD filled the house of God. (5:14).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 8:1-11: The same assembly in the seventh month, the ark carried up, and the cloud that stopped the priests serving.
Exodus 40:34-35: The cloud covers the tent of meeting and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle, so Moses cannot enter.
Deuteronomy 10:1-5: Moses puts the two stone tablets into the ark he made, and they are there still.
Numbers 10:1-10: Two silver trumpets are made for summoning the assembly and for sounding over the burnt offerings.
1 Chronicles 15:16-24: David appoints Heman, Asaph, and Ethan as singers and the priests to blow trumpets before the ark.

translationNotes.note: Verse 9 notes the carrying poles were long enough that their ends showed from in front of the inner room, though they could not be seen from outside. The poles were never to be removed from the ark's rings (Exodus 25:15). Once the ark had a permanent house, the poles it travelled on stayed in place anyway, visible to any priest who came as far as the curtain.

Verse 10 says there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets Moses put there at Horeb. The jar of manna and Aaron's rod were placed 'before the Testimony' rather than inside it (Exodus 16:33-34, Numbers 17:10), and Hebrews 9:4 lists all three together with the ark. The chest itself was a box of acacia wood overlaid with gold, about three and three-quarter feet long.

These are not the ram's horn shofar but straight silver trumpets, made by Moses' command in Numbers 10:1-10 and blown only by priests. Two were made in the wilderness; verse 12 has a hundred and twenty sounding together with the singers. Roman soldiers carried off a pair of these from the temple in AD 70, and they are carved on the Arch of Titus in Rome.

The inner room where the ark was set, a windowless cube twenty cubits on a side, about thirty feet each way, shut off by a curtain. Only the high priest entered it, once a year on the Day of Atonement with blood (Leviticus 16:2,34). Verse 7 is the last time in Scripture anyone carries the ark into it.

Verses 13-14 report the same thing that happened when Moses finished the tabernacle: the cloud filled it and the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34-35). Kavod is built on the root for weight, so the word carries the sense of something with real mass and presence rather than brightness. The text records the event; it does not describe what was seen.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon deposits David's dedicated treasures in the temple, then brings the ark of the covenant into the Most Holy Place with sacrifices and a large assembly; as priests and Levite musicians praise God, the cloud of the LORD's glory fills the temple so completely that the priests cannot continue their service.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 6
summaryBullets: Then Solomon declared: “The LORD has said that He would dwell in the thick cloud. (6:1).
But I have built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever.” (6:2).
And as the whole assembly of Israel stood there, the king turned around and blessed them all (6:3).
and said: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has fulfilled with His own hand what He spoke with His mouth to my father David, saying, (6:4).

‘Since the day I brought My people out of the land of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel in which to build a house so that My Name would be there, nor have I chosen anyone to be ruler over My people Israel. (6:5).
But now I have chosen Jerusalem for My Name to be there, and I have chosen David to be over My people Israel.’ (6:6).
Now it was in the heart of my father David to build a house for the Name of the LORD, the God of Israel. (6:7).
But the LORD said to my father David, ‘Since it was in your heart to build a house for My Name, you have done well to have this in your heart. (6:8).
Nevertheless, you are not the one to build it; but your son, your own offspring, will build the house for My Name.’ (6:9).

Now the LORD has fulfilled the word that He spoke. I have succeeded my father David, and I sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised. I have built the house for the Name of the LORD, the God of Israel. (6:10).
And there I have placed the ark, which contains the covenant of the LORD that He made with the children of Israel.” (6:11).
Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands. (6:12).

Now Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high and had placed it in the middle of the courtyard. He stood on it, knelt down before the whole assembly of Israel, spread out his hands toward heaven, (6:13).
and said: “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth, keeping Your covenant of loving devotion with Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts. (6:14).
You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David. What You spoke with Your mouth You have fulfilled with Your hand this day. (6:15).

Therefore now, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant, my father David, what You promised when You said: ‘You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your descendants guard their way to walk in My law as you have walked before Me.’ (6:16).
And now, O LORD, God of Israel, please confirm what You promised to Your servant David. (6:17).
But will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth? The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built. (6:18).
Yet regard the prayer and plea of Your servant, O LORD my God, so that You may hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You. (6:19).
May Your eyes be open toward this temple day and night, toward the place where You said You would put Your Name, so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place. (6:20).
Hear the plea of Your servant and of Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. May You hear and forgive. (6:21).
When a man sins against his neighbor and is required to take an oath, and he comes to take an oath before Your altar in this temple, (6:22).

then may You hear from heaven and act. May You judge Your servants, condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done, and justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness. (6:23).
When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading before You in this temple, (6:24).
then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel. May You restore them to the land You gave to them and their fathers. (6:25).

When the skies are shut and there is no rain because Your people have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your name, and they turn from their sins because You have afflicted them, (6:26).

then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants, Your people Israel, so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk. May You send rain on the land that You gave Your people as an inheritance. (6:27).
When famine or plague comes upon the land, or blight or mildew or locusts or grasshoppers, or when their enemies besiege them in their cities, whatever plague or sickness may come, (6:28).
then may whatever prayer or plea Your people Israel make— each knowing his own afflictions and spreading out his hands toward this temple— (6:29).
be heard by You from heaven, Your dwelling place. And may You forgive and repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart — for You alone know the hearts of men — (6:30).
so that they may fear You and walk in Your ways all the days they live in the land that You gave to our fathers. (6:31).

And as for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land because of Your great name and Your mighty hand and outstretched arm — when he comes and prays toward this temple, (6:32).

then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You. Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and they will know that this house I have built is called by Your Name. (6:33).
When Your people go to war against their enemies, wherever You send them, and when they pray to You in the direction of this city You have chosen and the house I have built for Your Name, (6:34).
then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause. (6:35).
When they sin against You— for there is no one who does not sin— and You become angry with them and deliver them to an enemy who takes them as captives to a land far or near, (6:36).

and when they come to their senses in the land to which they were taken, and they repent and plead with You in the land of their captors, saying, ‘We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly,’ (6:37).

and when they return to You with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them captive, and when they pray in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers, the city You have chosen, and the house I have built for Your Name, (6:38).
then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, their prayer and pleas, and may You uphold their cause. May You forgive Your people who sinned against You. (6:39).
Now, my God, may Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to the prayer offered in this place. (6:40).

Now therefore, arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might. May Your priests, O LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and may Your godly ones rejoice in goodness. (6:41).
O LORD God, do not reject Your anointed one. Remember Your loving devotion to Your servant David.” (6:42).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 8:12-53: The same dedication prayer, spoken from the same place before the altar.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The promise to David of a son who would build the house and a throne established forever.
Deuteronomy 12:5-11: The place the LORD chooses to put His name, where Israel is to bring its offerings.
Psalm 132:8-10: Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might, quoted in verses 41 and 42.
Daniel 6:10: Daniel opens his upper windows toward Jerusalem and prays on his knees three times a day.

translationNotes.note: Verse 13 has Solomon stand on a bronze stand five cubits square and three cubits high, about seven and a half feet on a side and four and a half feet tall, set in the middle of the court. He kneels on it in front of the whole assembly with his hands spread toward heaven. The detail is unique to Chronicles; 1 Kings 8:22 says only that he stood before the altar.

Six times in this prayer Solomon asks God to hear people who pray toward the temple from somewhere else: at war, in famine, in a foreign land, in exile. That is why Daniel opens his windows toward Jerusalem in Babylon (Daniel 6:10) and why Jews still face Jerusalem to pray. The direction is a claim about where God set His name, not about where God is.

Verses 32-33 make room in the prayer for a non-Israelite who comes from a distant land because he has heard of God's name, and ask that his prayer be answered too. This is not the resident alien living under the law, the ger, but an outsider with no covenant standing at all. The temple's outer court was open to such people, which is the court Jesus clears in Mark 11:15-17 quoting Isaiah on a house of prayer for all nations.

Verses 41-42 close the prayer with lines that stand in the Psalter: 'Arise, O LORD God, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might,' and the plea not to turn away the face of the anointed one. The same words appear at Psalm 132:8-10. 1 Kings 8 ends the prayer differently, so the two accounts preserve different closings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּרַשׂ כַּפָּיו (paras kappav), spread his palms
translationNotes.note: The standing posture for prayer in Israel was upright with the arms lifted and the palms turned up and out, which is what verses 12-13 describe before Solomon then kneels. It is the same posture at Exodus 9:29, Ezra 9:5, and 1 Timothy 2:8. Kneeling before a request of this size was the exception, and Chronicles records it because a king knelt in public.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon blesses the assembled Israelites, recounts how God chose Jerusalem and David's line, and offers an extended prayer at the bronze platform asking God to hear supplications made toward the temple in various circumstances - oath-taking, military defeat, drought, famine, plague, and captivity.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 7
summaryBullets: When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple. (7:1).
The priests were unable to enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD had filled it. (7:2).

When all the Israelites saw the fire coming down and the glory of the LORD above the temple, they bowed down on the pavement with their faces to the ground, and they worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD: “For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.” (7:3).
Then the king and all the people offered sacrifices before the LORD. (7:4).
And King Solomon offered a sacrifice of 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. (7:5).

The priests stood at their posts, as did the Levites with the musical instruments of the LORD, which King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD and with which David had offered praise, saying, “For His loving devotion endures forever.” Across from the Levites, the priests sounded trumpets, and all the Israelites were standing. (7:6).

Then Solomon consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD, and there he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, since the bronze altar he had made could not hold all these offerings. (7:7).
So at that time Solomon and all Israel with him— a very great assembly of people from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt— kept the feast for seven days. (7:8).
On the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for the dedication of the altar had lasted seven days, and the feast seven days more. (7:9).

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, Solomon sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the good things that the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel. (7:10).
When Solomon had finished the house of the LORD and the royal palace, successfully carrying out all that was in his heart to do for the house of the LORD and for his own palace, (7:11).
the LORD appeared to him at night and said to him: “I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for Myself as a house of sacrifice. (7:12).
If I close the sky so there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send a plague among My people, (7:13).
and if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land. (7:14).
Now My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayers offered in this place. (7:15).
For I have now chosen and consecrated this temple so that My Name may be there forever. My eyes and My heart will be there for all time. (7:16).
And as for you, if you walk before Me as your father David walked, doing all I have commanded you, and if you keep My statutes and ordinances, (7:17).
then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with your father David when I said, ‘You will never fail to have a man to rule over Israel.’ (7:18).
But if you turn away and forsake the statutes and commandments I have set before you, and if you go off to serve and worship other gods, (7:19).

then I will uproot Israel from the soil I have given them, and I will banish from My presence this temple I have sanctified for My Name. I will make it an object of scorn and ridicule among all the peoples. (7:20).
And when this temple has become a heap of rubble, all who pass by it will be appalled and say, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?’ (7:21).

And others will answer, ‘Because they have forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and have embraced other gods, worshiping and serving them— because of this, He has brought all this disaster upon them.’” (7:22).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 8:62-66: The same sacrifices, the same numbers, and the feast kept seven days and seven days more.
Leviticus 9:23-24: Fire comes out from before the LORD, consumes the offering, and the people shout and fall on their faces.
1 Chronicles 21:26: Fire falls from heaven on the altar at Ornan's threshing floor when David calls on the LORD.
1 Kings 9:1-9: The LORD appears to Solomon a second time and warns that this house will become a heap of ruins if Israel turns away.
Leviticus 23:33-36: The Feast of Booths, kept seven days from the fifteenth of the seventh month with a closing assembly on the eighth.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 has fire come down and consume the offerings the moment Solomon finishes praying. The same sign marked the start of sacrifice at the tabernacle (Leviticus 9:24) and at the threshing floor David bought for this site (1 Chronicles 21:26). The parallel account at 1 Kings 8:54-66 does not report it.

Verse 7 says Solomon consecrated the middle of the courtyard and offered there because the bronze altar could not hold that volume of offering. The altar was twenty cubits square (2 Chronicles 4:1), about thirty feet on a side, and even that was too small for the numbers involved, so the paved court itself had to be set apart for the day.

The dedication offerings in verse 5 total 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep over the fourteen days. The meat was not burned up: apart from the fat and blood, peace offerings were eaten by the people who brought them (Leviticus 7:15-16). This was the food supply for a national assembly camped at Jerusalem for two weeks.

The seven-day autumn feast of the seventh month, when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42-43). It is the third of the three pilgrim feasts that required every man to come to Jerusalem, and it fell right after the harvest was in. Solomon times the dedication to it, which is why the whole nation was already on the road.

translationNotes.term: The eighth day and the twenty-third
translationNotes.note: Verses 8-10 count out the calendar: seven days for the dedication, then the seven days of the feast, then the closing assembly on the eighth day, and the people sent home on the twenty-third of the seventh month. The atseret is the extra closing day commanded at Leviticus 23:36 and Numbers 29:35, a day of rest with its own offerings after Booths ends.

stories.keyTakeaway: Fire consumes Solomon's sacrifice and God's glory fills the temple; the people worship as Solomon dedicates it with massive offerings and a festival. Later God appears to Solomon at night, accepting the temple as his dwelling place but warning that Israel's unfaithfulness will result in destruction and exile.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 8
summaryBullets: Now at the end of the twenty years during which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own palace, (8:1).
Solomon rebuilt the cities Hiram had given him and settled Israelites there. (8:2).
Then Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and captured it. (8:3).
He built Tadmor in the wilderness, in addition to all the store cities that he had built in Hamath. (8:4).
He rebuilt Upper and Lower Beth-horon as fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars, (8:5).

as well as Baalath, all the store cities that belonged to Solomon, and all the cities for his chariots and horses — whatever he desired to build in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and throughout the land of his dominion. (8:6).
As for all the people who remained of the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites (these people were not Israelites) — (8:7).
their descendants who remained in the land, those whom the Israelites had not destroyed — Solomon conscripted these people to be forced laborers, as they are to this day. (8:8).
But Solomon did not consign any of the Israelites to slave labor, because they were his men of war, the leaders of his captains, and the commanders of his chariots and cavalry. (8:9).
They were also the chief officers for King Solomon: 250 supervisors. (8:10).

Solomon brought the daughter of Pharaoh up from the City of David to the palace he had built for her. For he said, “My wife must not live in the house of David king of Israel, because the places the ark of the LORD has entered are holy.” (8:11).
At that time Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of the LORD he had built in front of the portico. (8:12).

He observed the daily requirement for offerings according to the commandment of Moses for Sabbaths, New Moons, and the three annual appointed feasts — the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles. (8:13).

In keeping with the ordinances of his father David, Solomon appointed the divisions of the priests over their service, and the Levites for their duties to offer praise and to minister before the priests according to the daily requirement. He also appointed gatekeepers by their divisions at each gate, for this had been the command of David, the man of God. (8:14).
They did not turn aside from the king’s command regarding the priests or the Levites in any matter, including that of the treasuries. (8:15).
Thus all the work of Solomon was carried out, from the day the foundation was laid for the house of the LORD until it was finished. So the house of the LORD was completed. (8:16).
Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Eloth on the coast of Edom. (8:17).

So Hiram sent him ships captained by his servants, along with crews of experienced sailors. They went with Solomon’s servants to Ophir and acquired from there 450 talents of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon. (8:18).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 9:10-28: The same building projects, the same forced labour, and the same fleet sailing from Ezion-geber.
1 Kings 3:1: Solomon makes a marriage alliance with Pharaoh and brings his daughter into the city of David.
Deuteronomy 20:10-18: Distant cities may be put to forced labour, but the nations of the land are placed under the ban.
Numbers 28:1-31: The daily, sabbath, new moon, and festival offerings that verses 12 to 13 say Solomon kept up.
1 Kings 10:11-12: Hiram's fleet brings gold from Ophir along with almug wood and precious stones.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרֵי הַמִּסְכְּנוֹת (arei ha-miskenot), storage cities
translationNotes.note: Verses 4-6 name three kinds of royal town. Store cities held the grain, oil, and wine collected as tax and the stock for a campaign. Chariot cities kept the teams, the vehicles, and the men near level ground where they could be used. Fortified towns like Upper and Lower Beth-horon guarded the passes, in that case the climb from the coastal plain up to Jerusalem.

Verse 4 has Solomon build Tadmor in the wilderness. It is the oasis in the Syrian desert about 130 miles northeast of Damascus, later famous under its Greek name Palmyra. Nothing grows between it and the Euphrates, so whoever held the water there controlled the desert shortcut for caravans between Syria and Mesopotamia.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַס עֹבֵד (mas oved), labour levy
translationNotes.note: Verses 7-9 draw a line the reader should not miss. Descendants of the Canaanite peoples still in the land were conscripted into permanent labour gangs, while no Israelite was put in them; Israelites served as soldiers, officers, and chariot commanders. The distinction is by legal standing, not by ancestry alone, and Leviticus 25:39-43 forbids treating a fellow Israelite as a slave.

Verse 11 records Solomon moving his Egyptian wife out of the City of David into a house built for her, saying no wife of his should live where the ark of the LORD has been, because those places are holy. The verse states the reason plainly and does not comment further. 1 Kings 9:24 records the same move without the explanation.

Verse 18 gives the Ophir voyage's return as 450 talents of gold; the parallel at 1 Kings 9:28 gives 420. Both figures stand as written. A talent runs about 75 pounds, so either number is well over fifteen tons of gold, shipped from Ezion-geber at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba by Phoenician crews who knew the sea and Israelite crews who did not.

stories.keyTakeaway: After twenty years of building, Solomon completes the temple and fortifies cities throughout his territory; he uses non-Israelite descendants as slave labor while Israelites serve as military officials, establishes the temple sacrifices and priestly divisions, and sends a joint expedition with Hiram's ships to Ophir for gold.

stories.title: 👑 2 Chronicles 9
summaryBullets: Now when the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon, she came to test him with difficult questions. She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large caravan— with camels bearing spices, gold in abundance, and precious stones. And she came to Solomon and spoke with him about all that was on her mind. (9:1).
And Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for him to explain. (9:2).
When the queen of Sheba saw the wisdom of Solomon, the palace he had built, (9:3).

the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the service and attire of his attendants, the attire of his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he presented at the house of the LORD, it took her breath away. (9:4).
She said to the king, “The report I heard in my own country about your words and wisdom is true. (9:5).
But I did not believe the reports until I came and saw with my own eyes. Indeed, not half of the greatness of your wisdom was told to me. You have far exceeded the report I heard. (9:6).
How blessed are your men! How blessed are these servants of yours who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom! (9:7).

Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on His throne to be king for the LORD your God. Because your God loved Israel enough to establish them forever, He has made you king over them to carry out justice and righteousness.” (9:8).
Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, a great quantity of spices, and precious stones. There had never been such spices as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. (9:9).
(The servants of Hiram and of Solomon who brought gold from Ophir also brought algum wood and precious stones. (9:10).

The king made the algum wood into steps for the house of the LORD and for the king’s palace, and into lyres and harps for the singers. Never before had anything like them been seen in the land of Judah.) (9:11).
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all she desired — whatever she asked — far more than she had brought the king. Then she left and returned to her own country, along with her servants. (9:12).
The weight of gold that came to Solomon each year was 666 talents, (9:13).
not including the revenue from the merchants and traders. And all the Arabian kings and governors of the land also brought gold and silver to Solomon. (9:14).
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold; six hundred shekels of hammered gold went into each shield. (9:15).
He also made three hundred small shields of hammered gold; three hundred shekels of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. (9:16).
Additionally, the king made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold. (9:17).
The throne had six steps, and a footstool of gold was attached to it. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest. (9:18).
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at either end of each step. Nothing like this had ever been made for any kingdom. (9:19).

All King Solomon’s drinking cups were gold, and all the utensils of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. There was no silver, because it was accounted as nothing in the days of Solomon. (9:20).
For the king had the ships of Tarshish that went with Hiram’s servants, and once every three years the ships of Tarshish would arrive bearing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. (9:21).
So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. (9:22).
All the kings of the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart. (9:23).
Year after year, each visitor would bring his tribute: articles of silver and gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules. (9:24).
Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horses, which he stationed in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem. (9:25).
He reigned over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt. (9:26).
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills. (9:27).
Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from all the lands. (9:28).

As for the rest of the acts of Solomon, from beginning to end, are they not written in the Records of Nathan the Prophet, in the Prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the Visions of Iddo the Seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat? (9:29).
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. (9:30).
And Solomon rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place. (9:31).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 10:1-29: The same visit from the queen of Sheba, the same 666 talents of yearly gold, and the same ivory throne.
Matthew 12:42: The queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and something greater is here.
1 Kings 11:1-13: Solomon's foreign wives turn his heart away, and the kingdom is to be torn from his son.
Deuteronomy 17:16-17: The king is not to multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold for himself.
Psalm 72:10-11: The kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts, and all kings fall down before him.

translationNotes.note: A kingdom in southwest Arabia, in what is now Yemen, about 1,400 miles from Jerusalem by the overland incense road. Its wealth came from controlling the trade in frankincense and myrrh, which is exactly what the queen brings in verse 9 along with 120 talents of gold, roughly four and a half tons. The journey each way took months by camel caravan.

Verse 13 gives Solomon's yearly gold income as 666 talents, not counting trade and tribute. A talent is about 75 pounds, so that is roughly 25 tons of gold a year. The figure is the annual take of an empire sitting across the trade roads between Egypt, Arabia, and Mesopotamia, not a private fortune.

Verse 21 describes a fleet that sailed with Hiram's crews and came back once every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. The phrase names a class of large deep-water merchantman built for long hauls rather than a destination on every voyage. Scripture never locates Tarshish; Jonah 1:3 has a man buy passage there from Joppa to get as far away as a ship could take him.

Verses 17-19 describe a throne of ivory overlaid with gold, six steps, a gold footstool, a lion beside each armrest and twelve more on the steps. Ivory came up the same trade routes as the gold, and carved ivory panels inlaid into royal furniture have been excavated at Samaria and at Nimrud in Assyria. The six steps put the king physically above every person in the room.

translationNotes.term: The House of the Forest of Lebanon
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית יַעַר הַלְּבָנוֹן (bet yaar ha-Levanon)
translationNotes.note: The hall named in verses 16 and 20 got its name from its rows of cedar pillars, which stood like a forest inside it (1 Kings 7:2-5). It served as armoury and treasury: the 200 large and 300 small gold shields of verses 15-16 were stored there. Isaiah 22:8 calls it the place Judah looked to for weapons.

stories.keyTakeaway: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon, questions him, and is astonished by his wisdom and wealth; he gives her everything she asks for. Solomon's riches, military resources, and trading operations exceed all other kings, and people from everywhere bring him gifts to hear his wisdom.

stories.title: ➗ 2 Chronicles 10
summaryBullets: Then Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gone there to make him king. (10:1).
When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about this, he returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon. (10:2).
So they sent for Jeroboam, and he and all Israel came to Rehoboam and said, (10:3).
“Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you must lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.” (10:4).
Rehoboam answered, “Come back to me in three days.” So the people departed. (10:5).
Then King Rehoboam consulted with the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. “How do you advise me to respond to these people?” he asked. (10:6).
They replied, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (10:7).
But Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders; instead, he consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him. (10:8).
He asked them, “What message do you advise that we send back to these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’ ?” (10:9).

The young men who had grown up with him replied, “This is how you should answer these people who said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you must make it lighter.’ This is what you should tell them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist! (10:10).
Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.’” (10:11).
After three days, Jeroboam and all the people returned to Rehoboam, since the king had said, “Come back to me on the third day.” (10:12).
And the king answered them harshly. King Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders (10:13).

and spoke to them as the young men had advised, saying, “Whereas my father made your yoke heavy, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.” (10:14).

So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God, in order that the LORD might fulfill the word that He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat. (10:15).

When all Israel saw that the king had refused to listen to them, they answered the king: “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!” So all the Israelites went home, (10:16).
but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah. (10:17).
Then King Rehoboam sent out Hadoram, who was in charge of the forced labor, but the Israelites stoned him to death. And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem. (10:18).
So to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David. (10:19).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 12:1-19: The same assembly at Shechem, the same answer about scorpions, and the same revolt of the ten tribes.
1 Kings 11:26-40: Ahijah tears his new cloak into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten of them.
1 Kings 5:13-15: Solomon's levy of thirty thousand forced labourers, the burden Israel asks Rehoboam to lighten.
2 Samuel 20:1: Sheba son of Bichri raises the same cry: we have no share in David, every man to his tents.
Joshua 24:1,25: Joshua gathers all the tribes to Shechem and makes a covenant for them there before he dies.

translationNotes.note: The wooden beam laid across the necks of a pair of oxen so they pull together under a driver. Used of a nation, it means taxation and conscripted labour owed to a king, which is exactly what the elders ask Rehoboam to lighten in verse 4. Breaking a yoke is the standard picture for throwing off that burden (Jeremiah 28:10-11).

Rehoboam's answer in verses 11 and 14 contrasts whips with scorpions. The word names a scourge whose lashes carried barbs or metal beads that tore flesh rather than simply bruising it, so the reply promises a harsher instrument of the same kind. The image is a lash, not the animal.

A town about forty miles north of Jerusalem, in the narrow pass between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the north-south ridge road crosses the east-west route. Abraham built his first altar in Canaan there (Genesis 12:6-7), Joshua read the blessings and curses between the two mountains (Joshua 8:30-35), and Joseph's bones were buried there (Joshua 24:32). Rehoboam has to go north to Shechem to be made king, which already says who holds the leverage.

The shout in verse 16 is the old muster cry for breaking camp and going home, and it is a formal renunciation. Sheba son of Bichri used the identical words to pull the northern tribes away from David (2 Samuel 20:1). By the time the sentence is finished the northern tribes have withdrawn from the house of David, and the split runs for the rest of the Old Testament.

translationNotes.term: The officer over the forced labour
translationNotes.note: Verse 18 has Rehoboam send Hadoram, the man in charge of the labour levy, to the north, and they stone him to death. He had held the post since David's reign (2 Samuel 20:24) and through Solomon's building programme. Sending the tax and conscription officer to negotiate with men who had just asked for the burden to be lifted put the most hated office in the kingdom in front of a crowd.

stories.keyTakeaway: Rehoboam refuses to lighten Israel's tax burden, choosing harsh advice from his young counselors over the elders' counsel for mercy; Israel rebels and splits from his rule, stoning his labor officer and forcing him to flee to Jerusalem.

stories.title: ➗ 2 Chronicles 11
summaryBullets: When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he mobilized the house of Judah and Benjamin — 180,000 chosen warriors — to fight against Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam. (11:1).
But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God: (11:2).
“Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon king of Judah and all the Israelites in Judah and Benjamin (11:3).

that this is what the LORD says: ‘You are not to go up and fight against your brothers. Each of you must return home, for this is My doing.’” So they listened to the words of the LORD and turned back from going against Jeroboam. (11:4).
Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and he built up cities for defense in Judah. (11:5).
He built up Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, (11:6).
Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam, (11:7).
Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, (11:8).
Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, (11:9).
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, the fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin. (11:10).
He strengthened their fortifications and put officers in them, with supplies of food, oil, and wine. (11:11).
He also put shields and spears in all the cities and strengthened them greatly. So Judah and Benjamin belonged to him. (11:12).
Moreover, the priests and Levites from all their districts throughout Israel stood with Rehoboam. (11:13).
For the Levites left their pasturelands and their possessions and went to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them as priests of the LORD. (11:14).
And Jeroboam appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat demons and calf idols he had made. (11:15).
Those from every tribe of Israel who had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God followed the Levites to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers. (11:16).
So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and supported Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, because they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon. (11:17).
And Rehoboam married Mahalath, who was the daughter of David’s son Jerimoth and of Abihail, the daughter of Jesse’s son Eliab. (11:18).
She bore sons to him: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham. (11:19).
After her, he married Maacah daughter of Absalom, and she bore to him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith. (11:20).

Rehoboam loved Maacah daughter of Absalom more than all his wives and concubines. In all, he had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he was the father of twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters. (11:21).
Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, intending to make him king. (11:22).

Rehoboam also acted wisely by dispersing some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities. He gave them abundant provisions and sought many wives for them. (11:23).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 12:21-24: Shemaiah tells the 180,000 men mustered from Judah and Benjamin not to fight their brothers, and they go home.
1 Kings 12:25-33: Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and appoints priests who are not from Levi.
Leviticus 17:7: Israel is not to sacrifice any longer to the goat demons after whom they play the harlot.
Deuteronomy 12:13-14: Burnt offerings may be made only at the place the LORD chooses, not at every place you see.
2 Chronicles 13:8-12: Abijah tells Israel that Judah still keeps the Aaronic priests, the lampstand, and the daily offerings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרֵי מְצוּרוֹת (arei metsurot), fortified cities
translationNotes.note: Verses 6-12 name the ring Rehoboam built: Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam, Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. All of them lie south and west of Jerusalem, covering the approaches from Egypt and the Philistine plain, and none guards the northern border. Verse 11 lists what fortifying meant in practice: a commander, walls, and stores of food, oil, wine, shields, and spears.

The second city of the kingdom, on a mound in the Shephelah about twenty-five miles southwest of Jerusalem, guarding the road up from the coast. Amaziah was murdered there after fleeing Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 25:27). Sennacherib's assault on it in 701 BC is carved across a wall of his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, and the siege ramp his engineers piled against the southwest corner is still on the ground at the site.

translationNotes.term: The priests and Levites came south
translationNotes.note: Verses 13-14 record priests and Levites abandoning their towns and pasture across the northern kingdom and moving to Judah, because Jeroboam had thrown them out of the priesthood. Levites held no farmland of their own, only town plots and grazing attached to them (Numbers 35:2-5), so leaving meant walking away from everything they owned.

translationNotes.term: The calves at Bethel and Dan
translationNotes.note: Verse 15 refers to the calves Jeroboam made. He set one at Bethel, twelve miles north of Jerusalem on the ridge road, and one at Dan at the far northern springs under Mount Hermon, so that no northerner needed to go to Jerusalem to worship. His words at 1 Kings 12:28 repeat Aaron's at the golden calf, word for word (Exodus 32:4). A large stepped platform for such a sanctuary has been excavated at Tel Dan.

Verse 15 says Jeroboam appointed priests for the high places and for the seirim. The word means hairy ones or he-goats and names goat-shaped spirits worshipped with sacrifice; Leviticus 17:7 forbids it outright and Isaiah 13:21 pictures them dancing in ruins. This is not a figure of speech in the text; it names what the northern shrines were serving alongside the calves.

stories.keyTakeaway: Rehoboam assembles an army to reclaim Israel but obeys the Lord's command through Shemaiah to stand down; he then fortifies Judah's cities, receives priests and Levites who reject Jeroboam's idolatry, and establishes his household with multiple wives and sons, appointing Abijah as crown prince.

headings.text: Jeroboam Forsakes the Priests and Levites

stories.title: ➗ 2 Chronicles 12
summaryBullets: After Rehoboam had established his sovereignty and royal power, he and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD. (12:1).
In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem (12:2).
with 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and countless troops who came with him out of Egypt— Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites. (12:3).
He captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem. (12:4).

Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah who had gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and he said to them, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.’” (12:5).
So the leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (12:6).

When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah, saying, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but will soon grant them deliverance. My wrath will not be poured out on Jerusalem through Shishak. (12:7).
Nevertheless, they will become his servants, so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands.” (12:8).
So King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem and seized the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. He took everything, including the gold shields that Solomon had made. (12:9).
Then King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place and committed them to the care of the captains of the guard on duty at the entrance to the royal palace. (12:10).
And whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, the guards would go with him, bearing the shields, and later they would return them to the guardroom. (12:11).
Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned away from him, and He did not destroy him completely. Indeed, conditions were good in Judah. (12:12).

Thus King Rehoboam established himself in Jerusalem and reigned. He was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel in which to put His Name. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite. (12:13).
And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. (12:14).

Now the acts of Rehoboam, from first to last, are they not written in the records of Shemaiah the Prophet and of Iddo the Seer concerning the genealogies? There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days. (12:15).
And Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. And his son Abijah reigned in his place. (12:16).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 14:25-28: The same raid by Shishak, the loss of the gold shields, and the bronze shields made to replace them.
1 Kings 11:40: Jeroboam flees to Shishak king of Egypt and stays there until Solomon's death.
1 Kings 10:16-17: The two hundred large shields and three hundred small shields of beaten gold that Solomon had made.
Deuteronomy 28:47-48: Because you did not serve the LORD with gladness, you will serve your enemies in hunger, thirst, and want.
2 Chronicles 7:19-22: The warning that if Israel forsakes the statutes, God will pluck them from the land and make this house a byword.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִכְנַע (nikhna), to bow low, submit
translationNotes.note: The word turns this chapter. It appears at verses 6, 7, and 12, of the princes and then the king, and the root means to be brought low or to bring oneself low, the posture of a beaten party accepting terms. Chronicles uses it as the hinge in several reigns, of Hezekiah at 32:26 and of Manasseh in chains at 33:12, and it is the verb in the promise at 7:14.

The pharaoh who founded Egypt's twenty-second dynasty, known in Egyptian records as Shoshenq I, who reigned about 945 to 924 BC. A relief on the Bubastite Portal at the temple of Amun in Karnak lists the towns his army took on this campaign, and a fragment of a victory stele bearing his name was found at Megiddo. Verse 3 gives his force as 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and troops from Libya, Sukkiim, and Cush.

Verse 3 lists the contingents in Shishak's army. The Libyans came from the desert west of the Nile, and Shishak's own family line came out of that stock. Cush is the kingdom on the upper Nile south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan. The Sukkiim are named nowhere else in Scripture; the word is understood as a type of light desert troop.

Verses 9-11 record Shishak carrying off the gold shields Solomon had made, 200 large and 300 small, hammered from a total of about two and a half tons of gold (2 Chronicles 9:15-16). Rehoboam replaces them with bronze and puts them under guard, brought out when the king walks to the temple and returned to the guardroom after. The ceremony continues; the metal does not.

translationNotes.term: Serving Me and serving the kings
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 says the people will become Shishak's servants 'so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands.' One Hebrew word covers worship, temple duty, farm labour, and vassal obligation alike, so the sentence is a straight comparison of two masters using the same term for both. English has to pick a different word for each and loses the point.

stories.keyTakeaway: Rehoboam abandons God's law, prompting Shishak of Egypt to invade and plunder Jerusalem; after Rehoboam humbles himself, the LORD spares him from total destruction but leaves Judah subject to Egypt. Rehoboam reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem, does evil by not seeking the LORD, and is succeeded by his son Abijah.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Chronicles 13
summaryBullets: In the eighteenth year of Jeroboam’s reign, Abijah became king of Judah, (13:1).
and he reigned in Jerusalem three years. His mother’s name was Micaiah daughter of Uriel; she was from Gibeah. And there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam. (13:2).
Abijah went into battle with an army of 400,000 chosen men, while Jeroboam drew up in formation against him with 800,000 chosen and mighty men of valor. (13:3).
Then Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and said, “Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel! (13:4).
Do you not know that the LORD, the God of Israel, has given the kingship of Israel to David and his descendants forever by a covenant of salt? (13:5).
Yet Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, rose up and rebelled against his master. (13:6).
Then worthless and wicked men gathered around him to resist Rehoboam son of Solomon when he was young, inexperienced, and unable to resist them. (13:7).

And now you think you can resist the kingdom of the LORD, which is in the hands of David’s descendants. You are indeed a vast army, and you have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made for you as gods. (13:8).

But did you not drive out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites? And did you not make priests for yourselves as do the peoples of other lands? Now whoever comes to consecrate himself with a young bull and seven rams can become a priest of things that are not gods. (13:9).
But as for us, the LORD is our God. We have not forsaken Him; the priests who minister to the LORD are sons of Aaron, and the Levites attend to their duties. (13:10).

Every morning and every evening they present burnt offerings and fragrant incense to the LORD. They set out the rows of showbread on the ceremonially clean table, and every evening they light the lamps of the gold lampstand. We are carrying out the requirements of the LORD our God, while you have forsaken Him. (13:11).

Now behold, God Himself is with us as our head, and His priests with their trumpets sound the battle call against you. O children of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you will not succeed.” (13:12).
Now Jeroboam had sent troops around to ambush from the rear, so that while he was in front of Judah, the ambush was behind them. (13:13).
When Judah turned and discovered that the battle was both before and behind them, they cried out to the LORD. Then the priests blew the trumpets, (13:14).
and the men of Judah raised the battle cry. And when they raised the cry, God routed Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. (13:15).
So the Israelites fled before Judah, and God delivered them into their hands. (13:16).
Then Abijah and his people struck them with a mighty blow, and 500,000 chosen men of Israel fell slain. (13:17).
Thus the Israelites were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers. (13:18).
Abijah pursued Jeroboam and captured some cities from him: Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with their villages. (13:19).
Jeroboam did not again recover his power during the days of Abijah, and the LORD struck him down and he died. (13:20).
But Abijah grew strong, married fourteen wives, and became the father of twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. (13:21).
Now the rest of the acts of Abijah, along with his ways and his words, are written in the Treatise of the Prophet Iddo. (13:22).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 15:1-8: The same short reign of Abijah son of Rehoboam, and the war between him and Jeroboam.
Numbers 18:19: The offerings given to Aaron and his sons are a covenant of salt forever before the LORD.
2 Chronicles 11:13-15: The priests and Levites abandon their pasturelands in the north because Jeroboam cast them out.
Numbers 10:8-9: The priests sound the trumpets, and when Israel goes to war the blast brings them to remembrance before God.
