1 Kings 12:28-33: Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan, his feast in the eighth month, and the priests he made from any who would come.

translationNotes.note: Verse 5 says the LORD gave David the kingship by a covenant of salt. Salt preserves and does not spoil, and it was required with every grain offering (Leviticus 2:13). Sharing salt bound the parties, so the phrase means an agreement that does not decay; Numbers 18:19 uses it of the priests' portions.

Verse 4 puts Abijah on this hill in the highlands of Ephraim to shout across at the northern army. It stood near the border town of the same name in Benjamin's allotment (Joshua 18:22), a few miles north of Jerusalem in the broken country between the two kingdoms. Standing on high ground to address an enemy force was how a commander made terms heard before a battle, as at 2 Kings 18:28.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלֵּא יָדוֹ (mille yado), to fill the hand, to ordain
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 says anyone in the north who came with a young bull and seven rams could be made a priest. The Hebrew idiom for ordination is to fill the hand, and the law restricted it to Aaron's line on pain of death for any outsider who came near (Numbers 3:10, 18:7). Jeroboam kept the ceremony and dropped the qualification, so the office went to whoever could afford the offering.

The priests sounding the alarm in verse 12 are doing what Numbers 10:9 commands: when war comes in your land, sound an alarm on the silver trumpets and you will be remembered before the LORD. It is a set signal with a stated purpose, not a fanfare, and the sound is the cue for the war cry in verse 15.

Verse 2 names Abijah's mother Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. 2 Chronicles 11:20 and 1 Kings 15:2 name her Maacah daughter of Absalom. Both stand as written, and Chronicles carries name variants of this kind throughout. The king's mother was named in the accession notice because the office of queen mother carried rank at court.

stories.keyTakeaway: Abijah king of Judah addresses Jeroboam's larger northern army on Mount Zemaraim, denouncing his rebellion and idolatry; when fighting erupts, God routs Israel and Judah wins decisively, with Abijah capturing several towns and Jeroboam dying shortly after.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Chronicles 14
summaryBullets: Then Abijah rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. And his son Asa reigned in his place, and in his days the land was at peace for ten years. (14:1).
And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God. (14:2).
He removed the foreign altars and high places, shattered the sacred pillars, and chopped down the Asherah poles. (14:3).
He commanded the people of Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and the commandments. (14:4).
He also removed the high places and incense altars from all the cities of Judah, and under him the kingdom was at peace. (14:5).
Because the land was at peace, Asa built fortified cities in Judah. In those days no one made war with him, because the LORD had given him rest. (14:6).

So he said to the people of Judah, “Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, with doors and bars. The land is still ours because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought Him, and He has given us rest on every side.” So they built and prospered. (14:7).
Asa had an army of 300,000 men from Judah bearing large shields and spears, and 280,000 men from Benjamin bearing small shields and drawing the bow. All these were mighty men of valor. (14:8).
Then Zerah the Cushite came against them with an army of 1,000,000 men and 300 chariots, and they advanced as far as Mareshah. (14:9).
So Asa marched out against him and lined up in battle formation in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah. (14:10).

Then Asa cried out to the LORD his God: “O LORD, there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You, and in Your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, You are our God. Do not let a mere mortal prevail against You.” (14:11).
So the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites fled. (14:12).

Then Asa and his army pursued them as far as Gerar. The Cushites fell and could not recover, for they were crushed before the LORD and His army. So the people of Judah carried off a great amount of plunder (14:13).
and attacked all the cities around Gerar, because the terror of the LORD had fallen upon them. They plundered all the cities, since there was much plunder there. (14:14).
They also attacked the tents of the herdsmen and carried off many sheep and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem. (14:15).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 15:9-15: The same reforms of Asa, the removal of the idols his fathers made, and the silver and gold brought into the house.
Deuteronomy 12:2-4: Destroy every place where the nations served their gods, their altars, their pillars, and their Asherim.
Genesis 26:1-6: Isaac settles at Gerar during a famine, and the LORD tells him not to go down to Egypt.
2 Chronicles 16:7-9: Hanani reminds Asa that the Cushites and Libyans were a huge force handed over to him when he relied on the LORD.
Psalm 20:7: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.

translationNotes.note: A bamah was a raised open-air platform for sacrifice, usually on a hill or ridge, with an altar, a standing stone, and an Asherah pole. Israel was told to destroy the Canaanite ones (Deuteronomy 12:2-3) and to sacrifice only at the place God chose (Deuteronomy 12:13-14). Almost every king's summary in Kings and Chronicles is graded on whether he tore them down, and most did not.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִנָּה (tsinnah), body shield - מָגֵן (magen), buckler
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 splits Asa's army by equipment, and the Hebrew uses two different words. Judah's 300,000 carry the tsinnah, a tall shield covering most of the body, heavy enough that Goliath had a man to carry his (1 Samuel 17:7), paired with a thrusting spear. Benjamin's 280,000 carry the magen, a small round buckler strapped to the arm, which leaves both hands free for a bow.

Cush is the kingdom on the upper Nile south of Egypt, in what is now northern Sudan, whose troops served in Egyptian armies and who later ruled Egypt outright as the twenty-fifth dynasty. Verse 9 brings Zerah up the coast road to Mareshah with 300 chariots. Judah had beaten off an Egyptian pharaoh two reigns earlier and now faces an army from further south still.

A fortified town in the Shephelah about twenty-five miles southwest of Jerusalem, one of the fifteen Rehoboam had walled (2 Chronicles 11:8), sitting where the valleys from the coastal plain open toward the Judean hills. An invader coming from the southwest had to take it or leave it behind him. The mound is Tell Sandahannah, next to Beit Guvrin.

The town Asa's men pursue the Cushites to in verses 13-14, in the dry country between Gaza and Beersheba on the edge of the Negev. Abraham and then Isaac both lived there as resident aliens and both quarrelled with its king Abimelech over wells (Genesis 20:1-2, 26:1-22). It sits on the route back toward Egypt, which is the direction a beaten army from the south would run.

stories.keyTakeaway: Asa becomes king and spends ten years removing foreign altars and fortifying Judah's cities; when the Cushite Zerah attacks with a massive army, Asa calls on God and defeats him decisively, pursuing the Cushites to Gerar and collecting substantial plunder.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Chronicles 15
summaryBullets: Now the Spirit of God came upon Azariah son of Oded. (15:1).

So he went out to meet Asa and said to him, “Listen to me, Asa and all Judah and Benjamin. The LORD is with you when you are with Him. If you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you. (15:2).
For many years Israel has been without the true God, without a priest to instruct them, and without the law. (15:3).
But in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought Him, and He was found by them. (15:4).
In those days there was no safety for travelers, because the residents of the lands had many conflicts. (15:5).
Nation was crushed by nation, and city by city, for God afflicted them with all kinds of adversity. (15:6).
But as for you, be strong; do not be discouraged, for your work will be rewarded.” (15:7).

When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Azariah son of Oded the prophet, he took courage and removed the detestable idols from the whole land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim. He then restored the altar of the LORD that was in front of the portico of the LORD’s temple. (15:8).

And he assembled all Judah and Benjamin, along with those from the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who had settled among them, for great numbers had come over to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him. (15:9).
So they gathered together in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign. (15:10).
At that time they sacrificed to the LORD seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep from all the plunder they had brought back. (15:11).
Then they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and soul. (15:12).
And whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman. (15:13).
They took an oath to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouting, trumpets, and rams’ horns. (15:14).
And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn it with all their heart. They had sought Him earnestly, and He was found by them. So the LORD gave them rest on every side. (15:15).

King Asa also removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Asa chopped down the pole, crushed it, and burned it in the Kidron Valley. (15:16).
The high places were not removed from Israel, but Asa’s heart was fully devoted all his days. (15:17).
And he brought into the house of God the silver and gold and the articles that he and his father had dedicated. (15:18).
And there was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign. (15:19).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 15:13-14: Asa removes his mother Maacah from her position for making a repulsive image for Asherah, and burns it at the Kidron.
Deuteronomy 4:29-31: From there you will seek the LORD, and you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and soul.
Hosea 3:4: Israel will remain many days without king or prince, without sacrifice, pillar, ephod, or household gods.
Exodus 32:20: Moses burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes Israel drink it.
Leviticus 23:15-21: The Feast of Weeks in the third month, the season of the great assembly held here.

translationNotes.note: Verses 12-15 record a sworn national agreement, not a private resolution: the people bind themselves by oath, with trumpets and rams' horns sounding, to seek the LORD, and verse 13 attaches the death penalty to refusal. A berit was cut, sworn aloud, and witnessed, and it carried stated penalties like any treaty of the period. The scene deliberately repeats the covenant ceremonies at Sinai and Shechem (Exodus 24:3-8, Joshua 24:22-25).

A Canaanite goddess and also the wooden object that stood for her, a pole or carved tree set beside an altar at a high place. Verse 16 says Asa's grandmother Maacah made a repulsive image for her, and Asa cut it down, crushed it, and burned it in the Kidron. Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids planting one beside the altar of the LORD, and inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai show Israelites pairing her name with the LORD's, which is exactly the mixture the reforming kings are tearing out.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן מוֹרֶה (kohen moreh), teaching priest
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 describes Israel as having gone long stretches without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without the law. Teaching was part of the priest's job description, not an extra: Deuteronomy 33:10 has Levi teach Jacob God's rules, Leviticus 10:11 makes the priests responsible for instructing Israel in the statutes, and Malachi 2:7 says the people should seek instruction from the priest's mouth.

Verse 9 has people from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon settling in Judah in large numbers. Movement ran both ways after the split, and Chronicles keeps recording it: priests and Levites came south under Rehoboam (11:13-14), and Hezekiah later sends couriers north to invite what was left of those tribes to Passover (30:10-11). The border between the two kingdoms was political, and families crossed it.

Verse 16 removes Maacah from being gevirah, a formal office at the court of Judah and not just a family relation. The king's mother held rank, sat at his right (1 Kings 2:19), and is named in the accession formula of almost every king of Judah. Stripping Maacah of the title was a public act of state, which is why it is recorded alongside the burning of her image.

stories.keyTakeaway: Azariah prophesies to Asa that God will be with him if he seeks God, spurring Asa to remove idols and lead Judah and Benjamin in a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul. Asa deposes his grandmother Maakah for idolatry, brings dedicated treasures into the temple, and enjoys peace for the rest of his reign.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Chronicles 16
summaryBullets: In the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah. (16:1).
So Asa withdrew the silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and he sent it with this message to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus: (16:2).

“Let there be a treaty between me and you as there was between my father and your father. See, I have sent you silver and gold. Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.” (16:3).
And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, conquering Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali. (16:4).
When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work. (16:5).
Then King Asa brought all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. And with these materials he built up Geba and Mizpah. (16:6).

At that time Hanani the seer came to King Asa of Judah and told him, “Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped from your hand. (16:7).
Were not the Cushites and Libyans a vast army with many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, He delivered them into your hand. (16:8).

For the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him. You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war.” (16:9).
Asa was angry with the seer and became so enraged over this matter that he put the man in prison. And at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people. (16:10).
Now the acts of Asa, from beginning to end, are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. (16:11).
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa became diseased in his feet, and his disease became increasingly severe. Yet even in his illness he did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians. (16:12).
So in the forty-first year of his reign, Asa died and rested with his fathers. (16:13).

And he was buried in the tomb that he had cut out for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bier that was full of spices and various blended perfumes; then they made a great fire in his honor. (16:14).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 15:16-24: The same treaty with Ben-hadad, the same dismantling of Ramah, and Asa's diseased feet at the end.
Isaiah 31:1: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses and chariots instead of looking to the Holy One of Israel.
Jeremiah 17:5: Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD.
2 Chronicles 14:9-12: Asa's earlier cry to the LORD against Zerah's vast army, and the rout that followed.
Zechariah 4:10: The eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth, the line quoted by Hanani in verse 9.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 has Baasha fortify Ramah, about five miles north of Jerusalem on the central ridge road, to stop anyone going in or out of Judah. That road is the only good route along the spine of the hill country, so a fort at Ramah is a blockade on Judah's trade and on defectors heading south. Verse 6 has Asa carry off the stone and timber and use them to build Geba and Mizpah, moving the frontier back north.

The king of Aram, the Syrian state centred on Damascus, whose name carries Hadad, the Aramean storm god. Verses 2-4 have Asa empty the temple and palace treasuries to buy him out of his treaty with Israel and into an attack on Israel's northern towns, Ijon, Dan, and Abel-maim, up in the Huleh basin. Buying a third party into a war was ordinary statecraft, and it is what the prophet condemns in verse 7.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית הַמַּהְפֶּכֶת (bet ha-mahpeket), house of twisting
translationNotes.note: Verse 10 says Asa put the seer Hanani in prison. The Hebrew names a specific device, built on the root meaning to overturn or twist: a frame that clamped the feet, and sometimes neck and hands, holding the body bent in one position. Jeremiah was put in the same thing at the Benjamin Gate for a night (Jeremiah 20:2), and Paul and Silas at Philippi (Acts 16:24).

Verse 14 says they laid Asa on a bier filled with spices and made a very great fire in his honour. This was not cremation, which Israel did not practise; the body was buried in the rock-cut tomb and the fire burned spices as a public honour to the king. Jeremiah 34:5 promises Zedekiah the same rite, and 2 Chronicles 21:19 records that Jehoram was denied it.

Verse 1 dates Baasha's attack to Asa's thirty-sixth year, while 1 Kings 16:8 has Baasha dead by Asa's twenty-sixth. Judah and Israel did not count the same way: Judah began the regnal year in the autumn month Tishri and Israel in the spring month Nisan, one kingdom counted a king's partial first year and the other did not, and a son often ruled alongside his father for years before reigning alone. Edwin Thiele set the two systems out in The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings in 1951 and reconciled the synchronisms on that basis.

stories.keyTakeaway: Asa hires Ben-Hadad of Aram to attack Israel and stop Baasha's threat, but the seer Hanani rebukes him for relying on human allies instead of God; Asa imprisons Hanani and later dies of a foot disease without seeking the Lord's help.

headings.text: The Death and Burial of Asa

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 17
summaryBullets: Asa’s son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place, and he strengthened himself against Israel. (17:1).
He stationed troops in every fortified city of Judah and put garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured. (17:2).
Now the LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek the Baals, (17:3).
but he sought the God of his father and walked by His commandments rather than the practices of Israel. (17:4).
So the LORD established the kingdom in his hand, and all Judah brought him tribute, so that he had an abundance of riches and honor. (17:5).
And his heart took delight in the ways of the LORD; furthermore, he removed the high places and Asherah poles from Judah. (17:6).
In the third year of his reign, Jehoshaphat sent his officials Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the cities of Judah, (17:7).
accompanied by certain Levites — Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah — along with the priests Elishama and Jehoram. (17:8).
They taught throughout Judah, taking with them the Book of the Law of the LORD. They went throughout the towns of Judah and taught the people. (17:9).
And the dread of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that surrounded Judah, so that they did not make war against Jehoshaphat. (17:10).
Some Philistines also brought gifts and silver as tribute to Jehoshaphat, and the Arabs brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats from their flocks. (17:11).
Jehoshaphat grew stronger and stronger, and he built fortresses and store cities in Judah (17:12).
and kept vast supplies in the cities of Judah. He also had warriors in Jerusalem who were mighty men of valor. (17:13).
These are their numbers according to the houses of their fathers: From Judah, the commanders of thousands: Adnah the commander, and with him 300,000 mighty men of valor; (17:14).
next to him, Jehohanan the commander, and with him 280,000; (17:15).
and next to him, Amasiah son of Zichri, the volunteer for the LORD, and with him 200,000 mighty men of valor. (17:16).
From Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, and with him 200,000 armed with bows and shields; (17:17).
and next to him, Jehozabad, and with him 180,000 armed for battle. (17:18).
These were the men who served the king, besides those he stationed in the fortified cities throughout Judah. (17:19).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 22:41-46: The summary of Jehoshaphat's reign, his peace with the king of Israel, and the high places that remained.
Deuteronomy 6:6-9: These words shall be on your heart, and you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them at home and on the road.
Deuteronomy 31:9-13: Moses gives the law to the priests and commands that it be read to all Israel every seventh year.
Nehemiah 8:7-8: The Levites help the people understand the law, reading clearly and giving the sense so that they grasp it.
Malachi 2:7: The lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִרְאַת יְהוָה (yir’at YHWH), Greek: φόβος Κυρίου (phobos Kyriou), Aramaic: דְּחַלְתָּא דַּי־יָי (deḥalta d’ay-ya)
translationNotes.note: Awe/reverence that leads to obedience and justice; it fell on nations and guided judges.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּרַשׁ (darash, 'seek') / שׁוּב (shuv, 'turn'), Greek: ζητέω (zēteō) / ἐπιστρέφω (epistrephō), Aramaic: בָּעָא (baʿa, 'seek') / תּוּב (tuv, 'turn')
translationNotes.note: To pursue God earnestly and turn back to His ways; Jehoshaphat set his heart to seek the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek: ἔλεος (eleos), Aramaic: חֲסְדָא (ḥasda)
translationNotes.note: Covenant-committed kindness; the refrain sung in procession (20:21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּרָכָה (berakhah, 'blessing'), Greek: εὐλογία (eulogía), Aramaic: בִּרְכָא (birka)
translationNotes.note: Named for the blessing given after victory.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehoshaphat strengthens Judah militarily and spiritually by removing idols, sending officials to teach the Law throughout the towns, and stationing garrisons in fortified cities; surrounding kingdoms grow fearful and bring him tribute instead of attacking.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 18
summaryBullets: Now Jehoshaphat had an abundance of riches and honor, and he allied himself with Ahab by marriage. (18:1).
And some years later he went down to visit Ahab in Samaria, where Ahab sacrificed many sheep and cattle for him and the people with him and urged him to march up to Ramoth-gilead. (18:2).

Ahab king of Israel asked Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Will you go with me against Ramoth-gilead?” And Jehoshaphat replied, “I am as you are, and my people are your people; we will join you in the war.” (18:3).
But Jehoshaphat also said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire first for the word of the LORD.” (18:4).

So the king of Israel assembled the prophets, four hundred men, and asked them, “Should we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should we refrain?” “Go up,” they replied, “and God will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (18:5).
But Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire? ” (18:6).

The king of Israel answered, “There is still one man through whom we can inquire of the LORD, but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad. He is Micaiah son of Imlah.” “The king should not say that!” Jehoshaphat replied. (18:7).
So the king of Israel called one of his officials and said, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.” (18:8).

Dressed in royal attire, the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones at the threshing floor by the entrance of the gate of Samaria, with all the prophets prophesying before them. (18:9).
Now Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made for himself iron horns and declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.’” (18:10).
And all the prophets were prophesying the same, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph, for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” (18:11).

Then the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah instructed him, “Behold, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” (18:12).
But Micaiah said, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever my God tells me.” (18:13).

When Micaiah arrived, the king asked him, “Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should we refrain?” “Go up and triumph,” Micaiah replied, “for they will be delivered into your hand.” (18:14).
But the king said to him, “How many times must I make you swear not to tell me anything but the truth in the name of the LORD?” (18:15).
So Micaiah declared: “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, ‘These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.’” (18:16).
Then the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?” (18:17).
Micaiah continued, “Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing on His right and on His left. (18:18).
And the LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one suggested this, and another that. (18:19).
Then a spirit came forward, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ ‘By what means?’ asked the LORD. (18:20).
And he replied, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ ‘You will surely entice him and prevail,’ said the LORD. ‘Go and do it.’ (18:21).
So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you.” (18:22).
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah went up, struck Micaiah in the face, and demanded, “Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?” (18:23).
Micaiah replied, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” (18:24).
And the king of Israel declared, “Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son, (18:25).
and tell them that this is what the king says: ‘Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.’” (18:26).
But Micaiah replied, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” Then he added, “Take heed, all you people!” (18:27).
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. (18:28).
And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle. (18:29).
Now the king of Aram had ordered his chariot commanders, “Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel.” (18:30).

When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “This is the king of Israel!” So they turned to fight against him, but Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God drew them away from him. (18:31).
And when the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him. (18:32).

However, a certain man drew his bow without taking special aim, and he struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. So the king said to his charioteer, “Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!” (18:33).
The battle raged throughout that day, and the king of Israel propped himself up in his chariot facing the Arameans until evening. And at sunset he died. (18:34).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 22:1-40: The same council, the same four hundred prophets, the same word from Micaiah, and Ahab's death at Ramoth-gilead.
Deuteronomy 18:20-22: The prophet who speaks presumptuously is to die, and the test is whether the word comes to pass.
1 Kings 21:17-24: Elijah's sentence on Ahab, that dogs would lick his blood where they licked Naboth's.
2 Chronicles 19:1-3: Jehu the seer meets Jehoshaphat coming home and asks why he helped the wicked and loved those who hate the LORD.
2 Kings 8:16-18: Jehoram of Judah marries Ahab's daughter and walks in the way of the kings of Israel, the fruit of this alliance.

translationNotes.note: Named for the blessing given after victory.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָמֹת גִּלְעָד (Ramot Gilad), heights of Gilead
translationNotes.note: A fortified town east of the Jordan on the high tableland of Gilead, sitting on the King's Highway trade route and the frontier between Israel and Aram. It was one of the six cities of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43, Joshua 20:8). Three generations fight over it: Ahab dies here, his son Joram is wounded here (2 Kings 8:28), and Jehu is anointed here to destroy Ahab's house (2 Kings 9:1-6).

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah makes iron horns and says Ahab will gore Aram with them (verse 10). The horn is the standard Hebrew image for strength, taken from a bull driving with its head, and prophets often acted a message out instead of only speaking it. He is quoting Moses' blessing on Joseph, whose horns push the peoples to the ends of the earth (Deuteronomy 33:17).

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehoshaphat allies with King Ahab and agrees to attack Ramoth Gilead; when the prophet Micaiah contradicts four hundred other prophets by warning of disaster, Ahab imprisons him and goes to battle anyway, where he is mortally wounded by a random arrow.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 19
summaryBullets: When Jehoshaphat king of Judah had returned safely to his home in Jerusalem, (19:1).

Jehu son of Hanani the seer went out to confront him and said to King Jehoshaphat, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, the wrath of the LORD is upon you. (19:2).
However, some good is found in you, for you have removed the Asherah poles from the land and have set your heart on seeking God.” (19:3).
Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem, and once again he went out among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and turned them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. (19:4).
He appointed judges in the land, in each of the fortified cities of Judah. (19:5).
Then he said to the judges, “Consider carefully what you do, for you are not judging for man, but for the LORD, who is with you when you render judgment. (19:6).
And now, may the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery.” (19:7).

Moreover, Jehoshaphat appointed in Jerusalem some of the Levites, priests, and heads of the Israelite families to judge on behalf of the LORD and to settle disputes. And they lived in Jerusalem. (19:8).
He commanded them, saying, “You must serve faithfully and wholeheartedly in the fear of the LORD. (19:9).

For every dispute that comes before you from your brothers who dwell in their cities— whether it regards bloodshed or some other violation of law, commandments, statutes, or ordinances— you are to warn them, so that they will not incur guilt before the LORD and wrath will not come upon you and your brothers. Do this, and you will not incur guilt. (19:10).

Note that Amariah, the chief priest, will be over you in all that pertains to the LORD, and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, in all that pertains to the king. And the Levites will serve as officers before you. Act resolutely; may the LORD be with the upright!” (19:11).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 16:18-20: Appoint judges and officers in all your towns, and do not pervert justice, show partiality, or take a bribe.
Deuteronomy 17:8-13: Cases too hard for a local court go up to the priests and the judge at the place the LORD chooses, and their ruling binds.
Exodus 18:13-26: Jethro tells Moses to appoint able men who fear God as rulers over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
Leviticus 19:15: Do no injustice in judgment; do not favour the poor or defer to the great, but judge your neighbour fairly.
2 Chronicles 18:1-3: The marriage alliance with Ahab that Jehu the seer confronts the king about here.

translationNotes.term: Jehu son of Hanani the seer
translationNotes.note: Hebrew has three words for the office. Navi is the prophet, the spokesman; ro'eh and chozeh both mean seer, one who is shown things, and 1 Samuel 9:9 explains that the man now called a prophet used to be called a seer. This Jehu had already delivered a judgment on Baasha king of Israel (1 Kings 16:1-7), and his father Hanani had rebuked Jehoshaphat's father Asa and been put in the stocks for it (2 Chronicles 16:7-10).

The charge is about a specific alliance. Jehoshaphat had joined Ahab of Israel in the attack on Ramoth-Gilead described in the previous chapter, where Ahab was killed by an arrow shot at random (2 Chronicles 18:28-34). Ramoth-Gilead was a walled town east of the Jordan on the frontier with Aram, and control of it changed hands repeatedly across several reigns. The two houses were also joined by marriage, Jehoshaphat's son having taken Ahab's daughter (2 Kings 8:18).

Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, and the asherah of the Old Testament is her cult object: a wooden pole or a living tree set up beside an altar. Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids planting one next to the LORD's altar. They were not confined to country shrines; 2 Kings 23:6-7 records Josiah carrying the Asherah out of the temple in Jerusalem itself, burning it in the Kidron valley, grinding it to dust, and tearing down the quarters inside the temple where women wove hangings for her.

translationNotes.term: He appointed judges in each of the fortified cities
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁפְטִים (shophetim) - Hebrew: מַשֹּׂא פָנִים (masso panim)
translationNotes.note: This is the court system the law had already prescribed. Deuteronomy 16:18 requires judges and officers in every town, and Deuteronomy 17:8-13 sends any case too hard for a local court up to the priests and the judge at the central sanctuary, whose ruling is final. Verse 11 splits that appeal bench in two, the chief priest over matters of the LORD and the ruler of Judah over the king's matters. The phrase rendered partiality in verse 7 is literally a lifting of the face, and it repeats Deuteronomy 10:17 almost word for word.

The Hebrew is literally between blood and blood, and it is the technical phrase from Deuteronomy 17:8 for deciding whether a killing was murder or accident. Everything turned on the answer. A man who killed without intent could run to one of six cities of refuge, three west of the Jordan and three east, among them Bezer on the plateau, Ramoth in Gilead, Golan in Bashan, Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron, and stand trial there instead of being cut down at the roadside by the avenger of blood (Numbers 35:9-25; Deuteronomy 19:1-13; Joshua 20:7-8).

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehu the seer rebukes Jehoshaphat for allying with the wicked but praises his removal of Asherah poles; Jehoshaphat then appoints judges throughout Judah and a judicial council in Jerusalem to administer God's law fairly and without corruption.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 20
summaryBullets: After this, the Moabites and Ammonites, together with some of the Meunites, came to make war against Jehoshaphat. (20:1).
Then some men came and told Jehoshaphat, “A vast army is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the Sea; they are already in Hazazon-tamar” (that is, En-gedi). (20:2).
Jehoshaphat was alarmed and set his face to seek the LORD. And he proclaimed a fast throughout Judah. (20:3).
So the people of Judah gathered to seek the LORD, and indeed, they came from all the cities of Judah to seek Him. (20:4).
Then Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem in the house of the LORD in front of the new courtyard (20:5).

and said, “O LORD, God of our fathers, are You not the God who is in heaven, and do You not rule over all the kingdoms of the nations? Power and might are in Your hand, and no one can stand against You. (20:6).
Our God, did You not drive out the inhabitants of this land before Your people Israel and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham Your friend? (20:7).
They have lived in the land and have built in it a sanctuary for Your Name, saying, (20:8).

‘If disaster comes upon us— whether sword or judgment, plague or famine— we will stand before this temple and before You, for Your Name is in this temple. We will cry out to You in our distress, and You will hear us and save us.’ (20:9).

And now, here are the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, whom You did not let Israel invade when they came out of the land of Egypt. So Israel turned away from them and did not destroy them. (20:10).
See how they are repaying us by coming to drive us out of the possession that You gave us as an inheritance. (20:11).
Our God, will You not judge them? For we are powerless before this vast army that comes against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You.” (20:12).
Meanwhile all the men of Judah, with their wives and children and little ones, were standing before the LORD. (20:13).

Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah, a Levite from Asaph’s descendants, as he stood in the midst of the assembly. (20:14).

And he said, “Listen, all you people of Judah and Jerusalem! Listen, King Jehoshaphat! This is what the LORD says: ‘Do not be afraid or discouraged because of this vast army, for the battle does not belong to you, but to God. (20:15).
Tomorrow you are to march down against them. You will see them coming up the Ascent of Ziz, and you will find them at the end of the valley facing the Wilderness of Jeruel. (20:16).

You need not fight this battle. Take up your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf, O Judah and Jerusalem. Do not be afraid or discouraged. Go out and face them tomorrow, for the LORD is with you.’” (20:17).
Then Jehoshaphat bowed facedown, and all the people of Judah and Jerusalem fell down before the LORD to worship Him. (20:18).
And the Levites from the Kohathites and Korahites stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, shouting in a very loud voice. (20:19).

Early in the morning they got up and left for the Wilderness of Tekoa. As they set out, Jehoshaphat stood up and said, “Hear me, O people of Judah and Jerusalem. Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe in His prophets, and you will succeed.” (20:20).

Then Jehoshaphat consulted with the people and appointed those who would sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness. As they went out before the army, they were singing: “Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever.” (20:21).
The moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir who had come against Judah, and they were defeated. (20:22).

The Ammonites and Moabites rose up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, devoting them to destruction. And when they had finished off the inhabitants of Seir, they helped to destroy one another. (20:23).
When the men of Judah came to a place overlooking the wilderness, they looked for the vast army, but there were only corpses lying on the ground; no one had escaped. (20:24).

Then Jehoshaphat and his people went to carry off the plunder, and they found on the bodies an abundance of goods and valuables — more than they could carry away. They were gathering the plunder for three days because there was so much. (20:25).
On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, where they blessed the LORD. Therefore that place is called the Valley of Beracah to this day. (20:26).
Then all the men of Judah and Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat at their head, returned joyfully to Jerusalem, for the LORD had made them rejoice over their enemies. (20:27).
So they entered Jerusalem and went into the house of the LORD with harps, lyres, and trumpets. (20:28).
And the fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel. (20:29).
Then Jehoshaphat’s kingdom was at peace, for his God had given him rest on every side. (20:30).
So Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-five years. His mother’s name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi. (20:31).
And Jehoshaphat walked in the way of his father Asa and did not turn away from it; he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. (20:32).
The high places, however, were not removed; the people had not yet set their hearts on the God of their fathers. (20:33).
As for the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from beginning to end, they are indeed written in the Chronicles of Jehu son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel. (20:34).
Later, Jehoshaphat king of Judah made an alliance with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly. (20:35).
They agreed to make ships to go to Tarshish, and these were built in Ezion-geber. (20:36).

Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works.” So the ships were wrecked and were unable to sail to Tarshish. (20:37).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 6:28-31: Solomon's prayer that when trouble comes and Israel spreads out its hands toward this house, God will hear from heaven.
Exodus 14:13-14: Stand still and see the salvation of the LORD; the LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.
Deuteronomy 2:4-9,19: Israel is told not to contend with Edom, Moab, or Ammon, because their land was given to them as a possession.
Judges 7:19-22: Gideon's three hundred blow their trumpets and the LORD turns every man's sword against his fellow in the camp.
1 Kings 22:48-49: Jehoshaphat's ships of Tarshish are wrecked at Ezion-geber and never sail to Ophir.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִרְאַת יְהוָה (yir’at YHWH), Greek: φόβος Κυρίου (phobos Kyriou), Aramaic: דְּחַלְתָּא דַּי־יָי (deḥalta d’ay-ya)
translationNotes.note: Awe/reverence that leads to obedience and justice; it fell on nations and guided judges.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּרַשׁ (darash, 'seek') / שׁוּב (shuv, 'turn'), Greek: ζητέω (zēteō) / ἐπιστρέφω (epistrephō), Aramaic: בָּעָא (baʿa, 'seek') / תּוּב (tuv, 'turn')
translationNotes.note: To pursue God earnestly and turn back to His ways; Jehoshaphat set his heart to seek the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek: ἔλεος (eleos), Aramaic: חֲסְדָא (ḥasda)
translationNotes.note: Covenant-committed kindness; the refrain sung in procession (20:21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּרָכָה (berakhah, 'blessing'), Greek: εὐλογία (eulogía), Aramaic: בִּרְכָא (birka)
translationNotes.note: Named for the blessing given after victory.

A male descendant of Levi (excluding the Aaronic priestly line). Assisted the priests in temple service: music, gatekeeping, instructing the people, preparing sacrifices. The priest and Levite who pass by the wounded man in the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:31-32) make Jesus' point cut sharper; both were professionally obligated to help.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵין גֶּדִי (Ein Gedi), spring of the kid
translationNotes.note: A freshwater spring and waterfall on the western shore of the Dead Sea, about 1,300 feet below sea level, with sheer cliffs and caves above it. It is the only reliable water on that stretch of coast, so an army coming up from Edom around the south end of the sea has to stop there. From En-gedi the ascent of Ziz (verse 16) is the steep climb west onto the Judean plateau, which is where Judah waits for them.

The phrase names a class of vessel, not a destination: heavy deep-water cargo ships built for long hauls, the kind that traded with distant Tarshish. Verse 36 has Jehoshaphat build them at Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba, at the Red Sea end, for the Ophir run. They were wrecked in port before they sailed.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehoshaphat seeks God's help when armies from Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir threaten Judah; the Lord promises victory, and the allied armies destroy each other while Judah collects plunder. After returning to Jerusalem with celebration, Jehoshaphat reigns in peace, though he later makes a foolish alliance with Ahaziah that God destroys through shipwreck.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Chronicles 21
summaryBullets: And Jehoshaphat rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David. And his son Jehoram reigned in his place. (21:1).
Jehoram’s brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat, were Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah; these were all sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel. (21:2).
Their father had given them many gifts of silver and gold and precious things, as well as the fortified cities in Judah; but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn. (21:3).
When Jehoram had established himself over his father’s kingdom, he strengthened himself by putting to the sword all his brothers along with some of the princes of Israel. (21:4).
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years. (21:5).
And Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done. For he married a daughter of Ahab and did evil in the sight of the LORD. (21:6).
Yet the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant He had made with David, and since He had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever. (21:7).
In the days of Jehoram, Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah and appointed their own king. (21:8).
So Jehoram crossed into Edom with his officers and all his chariots. When the Edomites surrounded him and his chariot commanders, he rose up and attacked by night. (21:9).

So to this day Edom has been in rebellion against the hand of Judah. Likewise, Libnah rebelled against his hand at the same time, because Jehoram had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers. (21:10).
Jehoram had also built high places on the hills of Judah; he had caused the people of Jerusalem to prostitute themselves and had led Judah astray. (21:11).

Then a letter came to Jehoram from Elijah the prophet, which stated: “This is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: ‘You have not walked in the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or of Asa king of Judah, (21:12).

but you have walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and have caused Judah and the people of Jerusalem to prostitute themselves, just as the house of Ahab prostituted itself. You have also killed your brothers, your father’s family, who were better than you. (21:13).
So behold, the LORD is about to strike your people, your sons, your wives, and all your possessions with a serious blow. (21:14).
And day after day you yourself will suffer from a severe illness, a disease of your bowels, until it causes your bowels to come out.’” (21:15).
Then the LORD stirred against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and Arabs who lived near the Cushites. (21:16).

So they went to war against Judah, invaded it, and carried off all the possessions found in the king’s palace, along with his sons and wives; not a son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest. (21:17).
After all this, the LORD afflicted Jehoram with an incurable disease of the bowels. (21:18).

This continued day after day until two full years had passed. Finally, his intestines came out because of his disease, and he died in severe pain. And his people did not make a fire in his honor as they had done for his fathers. (21:19).

Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years. He died, to no one’s regret, and was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings. (21:20).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 8:16-24: The same reign of Jehoram of Judah and the same revolt of Edom from under Judah's hand.
Genesis 27:39-40: Isaac tells Esau he will serve his brother, but that he will break his brother's yoke from his neck.
2 Chronicles 18:1: Jehoshaphat makes the marriage alliance with Ahab that brought Athaliah into the house of David.
1 Kings 21:25-26: No one gave himself over to do evil like Ahab, urged on by Jezebel his wife.
Deuteronomy 28:27,59-61: The LORD will strike you with tumours and with lasting sicknesses not written in this book.

translationNotes.note: Verse 4 has Jehoram put all his brothers to the sword on taking the throne. Jehoshaphat had given them fortified cities and treasure (verse 3), which made every one of them a rival with a garrison. Wiping out the other claimants was standard practice in the period, and Chronicles records that Judah's king used it inside the house of David itself.

Verse 7 says the LORD would not destroy the house of David because He had promised to maintain a lamp for him and his sons. The image is the household lamp kept burning through the night so a home is never dark and never abandoned, and the same phrase carries the promise at 1 Kings 11:36, 15:4, and 2 Kings 8:19. It is the guarantee the line will not go out, stated at the exact point the line nearly does.

The kingdom descended from Esau, in the red sandstone highlands southeast of the Dead Sea, holding the copper mines and the caravan road to the Gulf of Aqaba. David had made it a vassal (2 Samuel 8:14), and Judah's access to the Red Sea port at Ezion-geber depended on it. Verse 8 records the revolt that took that road away, and the grudge between the two nations runs on to Obadiah.

Verse 10 reports a second revolt the same year, this one from inside the kingdom. Libnah was a walled town in the Shephelah on the western frontier facing Philistine country, and it was one of the towns given to the priests (Joshua 21:13). Losing Edom cost Judah the southern trade road; losing Libnah opened the western approach.

Verse 12 brings a written warning from Elijah the prophet. It is the only piece of writing from Elijah recorded anywhere in Scripture, and it is addressed from the northern kingdom into Judah, which is outside the territory the rest of his ministry covers. The letter states the charge and the sentence, and the chapter then records both carried out.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehoram becomes king after Jehoshaphat, kills his brothers, marries into Ahab's house, and leads Judah away from God; Elijah warns him of coming judgment, and the LORD brings Philistine and Arab invasions, disease, and death upon him. Jehoram dies in pain after eight years of reign, mourned by no one and buried without honor.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Chronicles 22
summaryBullets: Then the people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, the youngest son of Jehoram, king in his place, since the raiders who had come into the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah. (22:1).
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem one year. His mother’s name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri. (22:2).
Ahaziah also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in wickedness. (22:3).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for to his destruction they were his counselors after the death of his father. (22:4).
Ahaziah also followed their counsel and went with Joram son of Ahab king of Israel to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead. But the Arameans wounded Joram. (22:5).

So he returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds they had inflicted on him at Ramah when he fought against Hazael king of Aram. Then Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram son of Ahab, because Joram had been wounded. (22:6).
Ahaziah’s downfall came from God when he went to visit Joram. When Ahaziah arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab. (22:7).
So while Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he found the rulers of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who were serving Ahaziah, and he killed them. (22:8).

Then Jehu looked for Ahaziah, and Jehu’s soldiers captured him while he was hiding in Samaria. So Ahaziah was brought to Jehu and put to death. They buried him, for they said, “He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart.” So no one was left from the house of Ahaziah with the strength to rule the kingdom. (22:9).
When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she proceeded to annihilate all the royal heirs of the house of Judah. (22:10).

But Jehoshabeath daughter of King Jehoram took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the sons of the king who were being murdered, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Because Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, was Ahaziah’s sister, she hid Joash from Athaliah so that she could not kill him. (22:11).
And Joash remained hidden with them in the house of God for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. (22:12).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 9:14-29: Jehu's revolt at Ramoth-gilead and his killing of Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah.
2 Kings 11:1-3: Athaliah destroys the royal offspring, and Jehosheba hides the infant Joash in the temple for six years.
2 Kings 10:12-14: Jehu kills forty-two relatives of Ahaziah at Beth-eked of the shepherds on the road.
1 Kings 19:15-17: Elijah is sent to anoint Hazael over Aram and Jehu over Israel, and whoever escapes one sword the other will kill.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The promise that David's house, kingdom, and throne would be made sure forever.

translationNotes.note: Verses 3-4 explain Ahaziah's policy by his family. Jehoshaphat had married his son to Athaliah of the northern royal house (2 Chronicles 18:1, 21:6), and a royal marriage in this period was a treaty: it bound the two courts, their armies, and their religion together. By this chapter the king of Judah takes his counsel from his mother's family and goes to war alongside them.

The town in verse 5 sits east of the Jordan on the tableland of Gilead, on the road between Damascus and the Israelite heartland, which is why Israel and Aram fought over it for three generations. It was a Levitical town and one of the six cities of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43, Joshua 20:8). Ahab died attacking it (1 Kings 22:29-37), Joram was wounded there, and Jehu was anointed there to take the throne.

The commander anointed to destroy the house of Ahab (verse 7), who kills a king of Israel and a king of Judah in the same operation. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, found at Nimrud and now in the British Museum, shows a figure labelled Jehu bowing to the Assyrian king and bringing tribute, which is the only picture of a named Israelite king that survives from the ancient world.

Daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, married into the house of David by Jehoshaphat's alliance, and the only woman ever to rule Judah. When Jehu killed her son she killed every royal heir she could reach and took the throne for six years. One infant survived, hidden in the temple by the high priest's wife, and the line of David hung on that one child.

Verse 11 names the woman who hid the infant Joash: a daughter of King Jehoram, sister of the murdered king, and, Chronicles adds, the wife of Jehoiada the high priest. 2 Kings 11:2 gives her name in the shorter form Jehosheba and does not mention the marriage. That marriage is why she could hide a child in the temple precinct for six years.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ahaziah becomes king of Judah at twenty-two, follows the evil ways of Ahab's house at his mother Athaliah's urging, and is killed by Jehu during a visit to the wounded king of Israel; Athaliah then destroys the royal family, but Ahaziah's infant son Joash is hidden in the temple by his aunt Jehosheba for six years.

headings.text: Jehu Kills the Princes of Judah

stories.title: 🔥 2 Chronicles 23
summaryBullets: Then in the seventh year, Jehoiada strengthened himself and made a covenant with the commanders of hundreds — with Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri. (23:1).
So they went throughout Judah and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah and the heads of the families of Israel. And when they came to Jerusalem, (23:2).
the whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. “Behold, the king’s son!” said Jehoiada. “He must reign, just as the LORD promised concerning the descendants of David. (23:3).
This is what you are to do: A third of you priests and Levites who come on duty on the Sabbath shall keep watch at the doors, (23:4).
a third shall be at the royal palace, and a third at the Foundation Gate, while all the others are to be in the courtyards of the house of the LORD. (23:5).

No one is to enter the house of the LORD except the priests and those Levites who serve; they may enter because they are consecrated, but all the people are to obey the requirement of the LORD. (23:6).
The Levites must surround the king with weapons in hand, and anyone who enters the temple must be put to death. You must stay close to the king wherever he goes.” (23:7).

So the Levites and all Judah did everything that Jehoiada the priest had ordered. Each of them took his men— those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty— for Jehoiada the priest had not released any of the divisions. (23:8).
Then Jehoiada the priest gave to the commanders of hundreds the spears and the large and small shields of King David that were in the house of God. (23:9).
He stationed all the troops, with their weapons in hand, surrounding the king by the altar and the temple, from the south side to the north side of the temple. (23:10).
Then Jehoiada and his sons brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, presented him with the Testimony, and proclaimed him king. They anointed him and shouted, “Long live the king!” (23:11).
When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and cheering the king, she went out to them in the house of the LORD. (23:12).

And she looked and saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance. The officers and trumpeters were beside the king, and all the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets, while the singers with musical instruments were leading the praises. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and screamed, “Treason, treason!” (23:13).

And Jehoiada the priest sent out the commanders of hundreds in charge of the army, saying, “Bring her out between the ranks, and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” (23:14).
So they seized Athaliah as she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate on the palace grounds, and there they put her to death. (23:15).
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and the king and the people that they would be the LORD’s people. (23:16).
So all the people went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols to pieces and killed Mattan the priest of Baal in front of the altars. (23:17).

Moreover , Jehoiada put the oversight of the house of the LORD into the hands of the Levitical priests, whom David had appointed over the house of the LORD, to offer burnt offerings to the LORD as written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and song, as ordained by David. (23:18).
He stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the LORD, so that no one who was in any way unclean could enter. (23:19).

And he took with him the commanders of hundreds, the nobles, the rulers of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD and entered the royal palace through the Upper Gate. They seated King Joash on the royal throne, (23:20).
and all the people of the land rejoiced. And the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to the sword. (23:21).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 11:4-20: The same plan by Jehoiada, the same crowning of Joash by the pillar, and Athaliah's death.
Deuteronomy 17:18-20: The king is to write out his own copy of the law and read it all the days of his life.
Numbers 3:10: Only Aaron and his sons serve as priests; any outsider who comes near is to be put to death.
Deuteronomy 13:6-11: Anyone who entices Israel to serve other gods is to be put to death, and the hand of the witness comes first.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The oath that a son of David would sit on the throne, which this one hidden child now carries.

translationNotes.note: Verse 17 has the crowd tear down the temple of Baal in Jerusalem, smash its altars and images, and kill its priest Mattan in front of them. Baal was the Canaanite storm god, credited with the rain that made or broke a harvest; his worship ran on sacrifice and on ritual sex acts meant to secure fertility, and 2 Kings 17:17 and Jeremiah 19:5 record children burned as offerings on his altars. Athaliah brought the cult from her father's court in Samaria, and it had a state temple in the capital of Judah until this day.

Verse 16 has Jehoiada make a covenant between himself, the king, and the people that they would be the LORD's people. Kingship in Judah was contractual in this sense from the start: 2 Samuel 5:3 has the elders cut a covenant with David before anointing him. The order in this chapter is deliberate, first the covenant, then the tearing down of Baal's temple in the next verse.

Verses 4 and 8 set the coup on the sabbath, when the priestly and Levitical courses changed shift, and Jehoiada released nobody. That put both the incoming and the outgoing division inside the temple at once, roughly double the usual armed manpower, without a single unusual movement anyone outside could notice. The divisions themselves are the twenty-four courses set up in 1 Chronicles 24.

Verse 13 has Athaliah find the boy king standing by his pillar at the entrance. 2 Kings 11:14 adds that this was the custom, so the king had a fixed station in the temple court where he stood for public ceremonies, in view of the assembly. It is the same spot where Josiah later stands to read the covenant aloud (2 Chronicles 34:31).

Verse 11 says they put the crown on Joash and gave him the edut. The word means the covenant testimony, the written terms, and is used of the tablets in the ark (Exodus 25:16). A king of Judah was handed the law at his coronation because his rule was under it, exactly as Deuteronomy 17:18-20 requires.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jehoiada the priest organizes military protection around the young king, crowns him at the temple, and has the queen Athaliah executed when she opposes the coronation. He then leads the people to destroy Baal's temple and restore proper worship at the Lord's temple.

headings.text: Jehoiada Restores the Worship of the Lord

stories.title: 🔨 2 Chronicles 24
summaryBullets: Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem forty years. His mother’s name was Zibiah; she was from Beersheba. (24:1).
And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest. (24:2).
Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters. (24:3).
Some time later, Joash set his heart on repairing the house of the LORD. (24:4).

So he gathered the priests and Levites and said, “Go out to the cities of Judah and collect the money due annually from all Israel, to repair the house of your God. Do it quickly.” The Levites, however, did not make haste. (24:5).

So the king called Jehoiada the high priest and said, “Why have you not required the Levites to bring from Judah and Jerusalem the tax imposed by Moses the servant of the LORD and by the assembly of Israel for the Tent of the Testimony?” (24:6).
For the sons of that wicked woman Athaliah had broken into the house of God and had even used the sacred objects of the house of the LORD for the Baals. (24:7).
At the king’s command a chest was made and placed outside, at the gate of the house of the LORD. (24:8).
And a proclamation was issued in Judah and Jerusalem that they were to bring to the LORD the tax imposed by Moses the servant of God on Israel in the wilderness. (24:9).
All the officers and all the people rejoiced and brought their contributions, and they dropped them in the chest until it was full. (24:10).

Whenever the chest was brought by the Levites to the king’s overseers and they saw that there was a large amount of money, the royal scribe and the officer of the high priest would come and empty the chest and carry it back to its place. They did this daily and gathered the money in abundance. (24:11).

Then the king and Jehoiada would give the money to those who supervised the labor on the house of the LORD to hire stonecutters and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, as well as workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the LORD. (24:12).
So the workmen labored, and in their hands the repair work progressed. They restored the house of God according to its specifications, and they reinforced it. (24:13).

When they were finished, they brought the rest of the money to the king and Jehoiada, and with it were made articles for the house of the LORD — utensils for the service and for the burnt offerings, dishes, and other objects of gold and silver. Throughout the days of Jehoiada, burnt offerings were presented regularly in the house of the LORD. (24:14).
When Jehoiada was old and full of years, he died at the age of 130. (24:15).
And Jehoiada was buried with the kings in the City of David, because he had done what was good in Israel for God and His temple. (24:16).
After the death of Jehoiada, however, the officials of Judah came and paid homage to the king, and he listened to them. (24:17).
They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and idols. So wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs. (24:18).
Nevertheless, the LORD sent prophets to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them, but they would not listen. (24:19).

Then the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, who stood up before the people and said to them, “This is what God says: ‘Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.’” (24:20).
But they conspired against Zechariah, and by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD. (24:21).

Thus King Joash failed to remember the kindness that Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had extended to him. Instead, Joash killed Jehoiada’s son. As he lay dying, Zechariah said, “May the LORD see this and call you to account.” (24:22).

In the spring, the army of Aram went to war against Joash. They entered Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the leaders of the people, and they sent all the plunder to their king in Damascus. (24:23).

Although the Aramean army had come with only a few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army. Because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, judgment was executed on Joash. (24:24).

And when the Arameans had withdrawn, they left Joash severely wounded. His own servants conspired against him for shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and they killed him on his bed. So he died and was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings. (24:25).
Those who conspired against Joash were Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabitess. (24:26).

The accounts of the sons of Joash and the many pronouncements about him, and of the restoration of the house of God, are indeed written in the Treatise of the Book of the Kings. And his son Amaziah reigned in his place. (24:27).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 12:1-21: Parallel account of Joash repairing the temple.
Exodus 30:11-16: Census/atonement money used for the sanctuary.
Deuteronomy 13:1-11: Command to purge idolatry and falsehood.
Matthew 23:35: Jesus recalls Zechariah’s murder between temple and altar.
Hebrews 11:36-38: Saints martyred for righteousness, echoing Zechariah.

translationNotes.note: God’s empowering presence for prophecy and leadership.

Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joash’s reign shows the danger of shallow faith tied to a leader. Without Jehoiada, Joash turns to idolatry and sheds innocent blood, bringing God’s judgment.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Chronicles 25
summaryBullets: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan; she was from Jerusalem. (25:1).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not wholeheartedly. (25:2).
As soon as the kingdom was firmly in his grasp, Amaziah executed the servants who had murdered his father the king. (25:3).

Yet he did not put their sons to death, but acted according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded: “Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin.” (25:4).

Then Amaziah gathered the people of Judah and assigned them according to their families to commanders of thousands and of hundreds. And he numbered those twenty years of age or older throughout Judah and Benjamin and found 300,000 chosen men able to serve in the army, bearing the spear and shield. (25:5).
He also hired 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for a hundred talents of silver. (25:6).
But a man of God came to him and said, “O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel — not with any of the Ephraimites. (25:7).
Even if you go and fight bravely in battle, God will overthrow you before the enemy, for God has power to help and power to overthrow.” (25:8).

Amaziah asked the man of God, “What should I do about the hundred talents I have given to the troops of Israel?” And the man of God replied, “The LORD is able to give you much more than this.” (25:9).
So Amaziah dismissed the troops who had come to him from Ephraim and sent them home. And they were furious with Judah and returned home in great anger. (25:10).
Amaziah, however, summoned his strength and led his troops to the Valley of Salt, where he struck down 10,000 men of Seir, (25:11).
and the army of Judah also captured 10,000 men alive. They took them to the top of a cliff and threw them down so that all were dashed to pieces. (25:12).
Meanwhile the troops that Amaziah had dismissed from battle raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon. They struck down 3,000 people and carried off a great deal of plunder. (25:13).
When Amaziah returned from the slaughter of the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the Seirites, set them up as his own gods, bowed before them, and burned sacrifices to them. (25:14).
Therefore the anger of the LORD burned against Amaziah, and He sent him a prophet, who said, “Why have you sought this people’s gods, which could not deliver them from your hand?” (25:15).

While he was still speaking, the king asked, “Have we made you the counselor to the king? Stop! Why be struck down?” So the prophet stopped, but he said, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my advice.” (25:16).
Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent word to the king of Israel Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu. “Come, let us meet face to face,” he said. (25:17).

But Jehoash king of Israel replied to Amaziah king of Judah: “A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son in marriage.’ Then a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle. (25:18).
You have said, ‘Look, I have defeated Edom,’ and your heart has become proud and boastful. Now stay at home. Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall — you and Judah with you?” (25:19).
But Amaziah would not listen, for this had come from God in order to deliver them into the hand of Jehoash, because they had sought the gods of Edom. (25:20).
So Jehoash king of Israel advanced, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh in Judah. (25:21).
And Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his own home. (25:22).

There at Beth-shemesh, Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, the son of Jehoahaz. Then Jehoash brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate — a section of four hundred cubits. (25:23).

He took all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of God with Obed-edom and in the treasuries of the royal palace, as well as some hostages. Then he returned to Samaria. (25:24).
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived for fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel. (25:25).
As for the rest of the acts of Amaziah, from beginning to end, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel? (25:26).

From the time that Amaziah turned from following the LORD, a conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there. (25:27).
They carried him back on horses and buried him with his fathers in the City of Judah. (25:28).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 24:16: Children not to be put to death for fathers’ sins.
2 Kings 14:1-20: Parallel account of Amaziah’s reign.
2 Samuel 8:13-14: David’s victories over Edom in the Valley of Salt.
Proverbs 16:18: 'Pride goes before destruction.'
2 Chronicles 16:9: The LORD supports those whose hearts are fully His.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא בְּלֵבָב שָׁלֵם (lo b’levav shalem), Greek: οὐκ ἐν καρδίᾳ τελείᾳ (ouk en kardia teleia), Aramaic: לָא בְּלֵבָבָא שְׁלִים (lā b’levava shlim)
translationNotes.note: Partial devotion; outward conformity without full covenant loyalty.

translationNotes.note: Idols of Edom taken after victory; irony that Amaziah worships the gods of a defeated people.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חוֹחַ (ḥoaḥ, 'thorn/thistle') and אֶרֶז (erez, 'cedar'); Greek: ἄκανθα (akantha) and κέδρος (kedros)
translationNotes.note: Parable of arrogance: the weak challenging the strong, illustrating Amaziah’s folly.
