The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

stories.keyTakeaway: Amaziah begins well by obeying some of God’s law but turns to idols and pride. He defeats Edom, but then brings their gods home, ignores prophetic warning, and challenges Israel’s king. Judah is defeated, Jerusalem’s wall broken, treasures plundered, and Amaziah is later killed in conspiracy.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Chronicles 26
summaryBullets: All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. (26:1).
Uzziah was the one who rebuilt Eloth and restored it to Judah after King Amaziah rested with his fathers. (26:2).
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years. His mother’s name was Jecoliah; she was from Jerusalem. (26:3).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done. (26:4).
He sought God throughout the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God. And as long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success. (26:5).
Uzziah went out to wage war against the Philistines, and he tore down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. Then he built cities near Ashdod and among the Philistines. (26:6).
God helped him against the Philistines, against the Arabs living in Gur-baal, and against the Meunites. (26:7).
The Ammonites brought tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread as far as the border of Egypt, for he had become exceedingly powerful. (26:8).
Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the angle in the wall, and he fortified them. (26:9).

Since he had much livestock in the foothills and in the plain, he built towers in the desert and dug many cisterns. And since he was a lover of the soil, he had farmers and vinedressers in the hill country and in the fertile fields. (26:10).

Uzziah had an army ready for battle that went out to war by assigned divisions, as recorded by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer under the direction of Hananiah, one of the royal officers. (26:11).
The total number of family leaders of the mighty men of valor was 2,600. (26:12).
Under their authority was an army of 307,500 trained for war, a powerful force to support the king against his enemies. (26:13).
Uzziah supplied the entire army with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingstones. (26:14).

And in Jerusalem he made skillfully designed devices to shoot arrows and catapult large stones from the towers and corners. So his fame spread far and wide, for he was helped tremendously until he became powerful. (26:15).

But when Uzziah became powerful, his arrogance led to his own destruction. He was unfaithful to the LORD his God, for he entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense. (26:16).
Then Azariah the priest, along with eighty brave priests of the LORD, went in after him. (26:17).

They took their stand against King Uzziah and said, “Uzziah, you have no right to offer incense to the LORD. Only the priests, the descendants of Aaron, are consecrated to burn incense. Leave the sanctuary, for you have acted unfaithfully; you will not receive honor from the LORD God.” (26:18).

Uzziah, with a censer in his hand to offer incense, was enraged. But while he raged against the priests in their presence in the house of the LORD before the altar of incense, leprosy broke out on his forehead. (26:19).
When Azariah the chief priest and all the priests turned to him and saw his leprous forehead, they rushed him out. Indeed, he himself hurried to get out, because the LORD had afflicted him. (26:20).

So King Uzziah was a leper until the day of his death. He lived in isolation, leprous and cut off from the house of the LORD, while his son Jotham had charge of the royal palace and governed the people of the land. (26:21).
As for the rest of the acts of Uzziah, from beginning to end, they are recorded by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz. (26:22).
And Uzziah rested with his fathers and was buried near them in a field of burial that belonged to the kings, for the people said, “He was a leper.” And his son Jotham reigned in his place. (26:23).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 15:1-7: Parallel account of Uzziah (Azariah).
Leviticus 10:1-3: Nadab and Abihu judged for unauthorized incense.
Numbers 18:7: Only priests to serve at the altar.
Isaiah 6:1: Isaiah’s vision of the LORD in the year King Uzziah died.
Proverbs 29:23: 'Pride brings a man low.'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֻזִּיָּה (ʿUziyya, 'My strength is Yahweh') / עֲזַרְיָה (ʿAzarya, 'Yahweh has helped'), Greek: Οζίας (Ozias) / Αζαρίας (Azarias), Aramaic: עֻזִיָּה (ʿUziya) / עֲזַרְיָה (ʿAzarya)
translationNotes.note: Two forms of his name appear; both emphasize God’s strength/help.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צָרַעַת (ṣāra‘at), Greek: λέπρα (lepra), Aramaic: גַּרְבָּא (garba)
translationNotes.note: Skin disease rendering one ritually unclean; here symbolic of pride and divine judgment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְטֹרֶת (qeṭoret), Greek: θυμίαμα (thymiama), Aramaic: קְטוֹרָא (qeṭora)
translationNotes.note: Fragrant smoke offered as worship; strictly limited to priests.

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

stories.keyTakeaway: Uzziah prospers as long as he seeks God, expanding Judah’s power and developing its defenses. When strong, he grows proud and unlawfully burns incense in the temple. God strikes him with leprosy, and he lives isolated until death.

stories.title: 🏛️ 2 Chronicles 27
summaryBullets: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerushah daughter of Zadok. (27:1).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. In addition, he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still behaved corruptly. (27:2).
Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD, and he worked extensively on the wall at the hill of Ophel. (27:3).
He also built cities in the hill country of Judah and fortresses and towers in the forests. (27:4).

Jotham waged war against the king of the Ammonites and defeated them, and that year they gave him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley. They paid him the same in the second and third years. (27:5).
So Jotham grew powerful because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God. (27:6).
As for the rest of the acts of Jotham, along with all his wars and his ways, they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. (27:7).
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. (27:8).
And Jotham rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. And his son Ahaz reigned in his place. (27:9).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 15:32-38: Parallel account of Jotham’s reign.
Micah 1:1: Micah prophesied during Jotham’s time.
Proverbs 16:3: Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will succeed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָעֹפֶל (ha-ʿOphel), Greek: Ὀφηλ (Ophel), Aramaic: עוֹפֵל (ʿOphel)
translationNotes.note: A fortified part of Jerusalem, south of the temple mount, used for defense and administration.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְחָה (minḥah), Greek: φόρος (phoros), Aramaic: מִנְחָא (minḥa)
translationNotes.note: A payment or offering acknowledging subjugation or alliance.
