A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.
The largest biblical dry measure, about 58 gallons or 220 liters; equivalent to ten ephahs. The unjust steward (Luke 16:7) discounts 'a hundred measures of wheat'; 100 kors, about 22,000 liters.

Ten thousand; also used idiomatically for 'countless.' Revelation 5:11's 'ten thousands of ten thousands' (myriades myriadon) of angels could be 100 million as a literal floor, though the intent is more naturally read as 'innumerable.'

stories.keyTakeaway: Jotham rules rightly before God, builds fortifications, and defeats the Ammonites who pay tribute. Though the people continue corruptly, he becomes mighty because he orders his ways before the LORD.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Chronicles 28
summaryBullets: Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD. (28:1).
Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even made cast images of the Baals. (28:2).
Moreover, Ahaz burned incense in the Valley of Ben-hinnom and sacrificed his sons in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. (28:3).
And he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree. (28:4).

So the LORD his God delivered Ahaz into the hand of the king of Aram, who attacked him and took many captives to Damascus. Ahaz was also delivered into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with great force. (28:5).
For in one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah. This happened because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. (28:6).
Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the son of the king, Azrikam the governor of the palace, and Elkanah the second to the king. (28:7).
Then the Israelites took 200,000 captives from their kinsmen— women, sons, and daughters. They also carried off a great deal of plunder and brought it to Samaria. (28:8).

But a prophet of the LORD named Oded was there, and he went out to meet the army that returned to Samaria. “Look,” he said to them, “because of His wrath against Judah, the LORD, the God of your fathers, has delivered them into your hand. But you have slaughtered them in a rage that reaches up to heaven. (28:9).
And now you intend to reduce to slavery the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem. But are you not also guilty before the LORD your God? (28:10).
Now therefore, listen to me and return the captives you took from your kinsmen, for the fierce anger of the LORD is upon you.” (28:11).

Then some of the leaders of the Ephraimites— Azariah son of Jehohanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai— stood in opposition to those arriving from the war. (28:12).

“You must not bring the captives here,” they said, “for you are proposing to bring guilt upon us from the LORD and to add to our sins and our guilt. For our guilt is great, and fierce anger is upon Israel.” (28:13).
So the armed men left the captives and the plunder before the leaders and all the assembly. (28:14).

Then the men who were designated by name arose, took charge of the captives, and provided from the plunder clothing for the naked. They clothed them, gave them sandals and food and drink, anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys. So they brought them to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria. (28:15).
At that time King Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria. (28:16).
The Edomites had again come and attacked Judah and carried away captives. (28:17).

The Philistines had also raided the cities of the foothills and the Negev of Judah, capturing and occupying Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, as well as Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo with their villages. (28:18).
For the LORD humbled Judah because Ahaz king of Israel had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been most unfaithful to the LORD. (28:19).
Then Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came to Ahaz but afflicted him rather than strengthening him. (28:20).
Although Ahaz had taken a portion from the house of the LORD, from the royal palace, and from the princes and had presented it to the king of Assyria, it did not help him. (28:21).
In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD. (28:22).

He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, who had defeated him, and he said, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” But these gods were the downfall of Ahaz and of all Israel. (28:23).
Then Ahaz gathered up the articles of the house of God, cut them into pieces, shut the doors of the house of the LORD, and set up altars of his own on every street corner in Jerusalem. (28:24).
In every city of Judah he built high places to offer incense to other gods, and so he provoked the LORD, the God of his fathers. (28:25).
As for the rest of the acts of Ahaz and all his ways, from beginning to end, they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. (28:26).
And Ahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of Jerusalem, but he was not placed in the tombs of the kings of Israel. And his son Hezekiah reigned in his place. (28:27).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 16:1-20: Parallel account of Ahaz’s reign.
Deuteronomy 12:29-31: Warning not to worship God in the abominable ways of the nations, including child sacrifice.
Jeremiah 7:31: Condemnation of burning children in the Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna).
Isaiah 7:1-14: Prophecy given during Ahaz’s reign: the virgin will conceive and bear a son (Immanuel prophecy).
2 Chronicles 7:14: God promises healing if His people humble themselves and turn from wickedness (contrast with Ahaz).

translationNotes.term: Shut the doors of the house of the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סָגַר דַּלְתוֹת בֵּית־יְהוָה (sagar daltot beit-YHWH); Greek: ἔκλεισεν τὰς θύρας τοῦ οἴκου Κυρίου (ekleisen tas thyras tou oikou Kyriou)
translationNotes.note: A symbolic and physical act of rejecting God’s worship in Jerusalem.

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.term: Molech and the Valley of Hinnom
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹלֶךְ (Molekh) - גֵּי בֶן־הִנֹּם (Gei Ven-Hinnom) - תֹּפֶת (Tofet)
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 says Ahaz burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom. The valley runs along the south and west edge of Jerusalem, and the burning ground in it was called the Tophet. Children were put into the fire before an image of Molech, the god of Ammon; Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5 set death as the penalty, and Jeremiah 7:31 says God never commanded it and it never came into His mind. The Greek form of that valley's name, Gehenna, is the word Jesus uses for hell (Mark 9:43-48).

Verse 23 gives Ahaz's reasoning: the gods of Aram helped Aram beat him, so he sacrificed to them. This was ordinary ancient thinking, that each nation's god held its own ground and won its own wars, and that a defeat meant you had backed the weaker god. 2 Kings 16:10-16 adds that Ahaz saw an altar at Damascus, sent the plan back to Jerusalem, and had a copy built for the temple court.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ahaz leads Judah into idolatry, even burning his sons in fire. Enemies defeat Judah, taking captives, though some are mercifully returned. He appeals to Assyria but is further oppressed. In distress he shuts the temple, builds altars everywhere, and dies in disgrace.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 29
summaryBullets: Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah. (29:1).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done. (29:2).
In the first month of the first year of his reign, Hezekiah opened and repaired the doors of the house of the LORD. (29:3).
Then he brought in the priests and Levites and gathered them in the square on the east side. (29:4).
“Listen to me, O Levites,” he said. “Consecrate yourselves now and consecrate the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers. Remove from the Holy Place every impurity. (29:5).
For our fathers were unfaithful and did evil in the sight of the LORD our God. They abandoned Him, turned their faces away from the dwelling place of the LORD, and turned their backs on Him. (29:6).
They also shut the doors of the portico and extinguished the lamps. They did not burn incense or present burnt offerings in the Holy Place of the God of Israel. (29:7).
Therefore, the wrath of the LORD has fallen upon Judah and Jerusalem, and He has made them an object of terror, horror, and scorn, as you can see with your own eyes. (29:8).
For behold, this is why our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and daughters and wives are in captivity. (29:9).
Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, so that His fierce anger will turn away from us. (29:10).
Now, my sons, do not be negligent, for the LORD has chosen you to stand before Him, to serve Him, to minister before Him, and to burn incense.” (29:11).

Then the Levites set to work: Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah from the Kohathites; Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel from the Merarites; Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah from the Gershonites; (29:12).
Shimri and Jeuel from the Elizaphanites; Zechariah and Mattaniah from the Asaphites; (29:13).
Jehiel and Shimei from the Hemanites; and Shemaiah and Uzziel from the Jeduthunites. (29:14).
When they had assembled their brothers and consecrated themselves, they went in to cleanse the house of the LORD, according to the command of the king by the words of the LORD. (29:15).

So the priests went inside the house of the LORD to cleanse it, and they brought out to the courtyard all the unclean things that they found in the temple of the LORD. Then the Levites took these things and carried them out to the Kidron Valley. (29:16).

They began the consecration on the first day of the first month, and on the eighth day of the month they reached the portico of the LORD. For eight more days they consecrated the house of the LORD itself, finishing on the sixteenth day of the first month. (29:17).

Then they went in to King Hezekiah and reported, “We have cleansed the entire house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the table of the showbread with all its utensils. (29:18).
Moreover, we have prepared and consecrated all the articles that King Ahaz in his unfaithfulness cast aside during his reign. They are now in front of the altar of the LORD.” (29:19).
Early the next morning King Hezekiah gathered the city officials and went up to the house of the LORD. (29:20).

They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. And the king commanded the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the LORD. (29:21).

So they slaughtered the bulls, and the priests took the blood and splattered it on the altar. They slaughtered the rams and splattered the blood on the altar. And they slaughtered the lambs and splattered the blood on the altar. (29:22).
Then they brought the goats for the sin offering before the king and the assembly, who laid their hands on them. (29:23).

And the priests slaughtered the goats and put their blood on the altar for a sin offering, to make atonement for all Israel, because the king had ordered the burnt offering and the sin offering for all Israel. (29:24).

Hezekiah stationed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres according to the command of David, of Gad the king’s seer, and of Nathan the prophet. For the command had come from the LORD through His prophets. (29:25).
The Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. (29:26).

And Hezekiah ordered that the burnt offering be sacrificed on the altar. When the burnt offering began, the song of the LORD and the trumpets began as well, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel. (29:27).
The whole assembly was worshiping, the singers were singing, and the trumpeters were playing. All this continued until the burnt offering was completed. (29:28).
When the offerings were completed, the king and all those present with him bowed down and worshiped. (29:29).

Then King Hezekiah and his officials ordered the Levites to sing praises to the LORD in the words of David and of Asaph the seer. So they sang praises with gladness and bowed down and worshiped. (29:30).

Then Hezekiah said, “Now that you have consecrated yourselves to the LORD, come near and bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD.” So the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all whose hearts were willing brought burnt offerings. (29:31).
The number of burnt offerings the assembly brought was seventy bulls, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs; all these were for a burnt offering to the LORD. (29:32).
And the consecrated offerings were six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep. (29:33).

However, since there were not enough priests to skin all the burnt offerings, their Levite brothers helped them until the work was finished and until the priests had consecrated themselves. For the Levites had been more diligent in consecrating themselves than the priests had been. (29:34).

Furthermore, the burnt offerings were abundant, along with the fat of the peace offerings and the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. So the service of the house of the LORD was established. (29:35).
Then Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced at what God had prepared for the people, because everything had been accomplished so quickly. (29:36).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:1-8: The same accession of Hezekiah, his removal of the high places, and the breaking of the bronze serpent.
2 Chronicles 28:24: Ahaz cuts up the vessels of the house of God, shuts its doors, and makes himself altars on every corner of Jerusalem.
Leviticus 4:13-21: The sin offering required when the whole assembly of Israel sins unintentionally.
Numbers 8:5-22: The cleansing of the Levites and their presentation before the LORD in place of Israel's firstborn.
1 Chronicles 25:1-6: David and the commanders set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals.

translationNotes.note: The word runs through the chapter and covers two different jobs. Applied to the building and its vessels it means scrubbing out and carrying off everything unclean, which is the physical work of verses 15-19. Applied to a man it means putting himself through washing, changed clothing, and abstention until he is fit to handle holy things (Exodus 19:10-15, Leviticus 8:6-13). Verse 34 records that the priests were slower at the second than the Levites were.

Verse 17 dates the work precisely: begun on the first day of the first month, the porch reached on the eighth, the house itself finished on the sixteenth. Passover falls on the fourteenth of that month (Leviticus 23:5), so the temple was still unclean when the date passed. That is the reason for the decision recorded in the next chapter.

Verse 21 brings seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats, offered for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. In the hattat the blood is put on the altar rather than the animal simply burned, because the rite is about cleansing what the sin has defiled (Leviticus 4). Verse 23 has the king and the assembly lay hands on the goats, the gesture that identifies the offerer with the animal.

Verse 34 records too few priests consecrated to skin the burnt offerings, so Levites stepped in. Flaying and cutting up the animal was assigned work (Leviticus 1:6), and the division of labour between priest and Levite was not casual. The verse states plainly that the Levites had been more diligent in consecrating themselves than the priests.

The deep ravine running along the east side of Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives, dry except in winter rains. It was the city's dumping ground for anything defiled, which is why every reforming king burns idols there and throws the ash into it (1 Kings 15:13, 2 Kings 23:4-6). David crossed it fleeing Absalom, and Jesus crossed it going to Gethsemane (2 Samuel 15:23, John 18:1).

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah becomes king at twenty-five and orders the temple doors opened and repaired; he directs the Levites to consecrate themselves and purify the sanctuary, which they complete in sixteen days. He then leads a massive sacrifice ceremony with animals brought by the assembly, and the temple service is restored.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 30
summaryBullets: Then Hezekiah sent word throughout all Israel and Judah, and he also wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh inviting them to come to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem to keep the Passover of the LORD, the God of Israel. (30:1).
For the king and his officials and the whole assembly in Jerusalem had decided to keep the Passover in the second month, (30:2).
since they had been unable to keep it at the regular time, because not enough priests had consecrated themselves and the people had not been gathered in Jerusalem. (30:3).
This plan pleased the king and the whole assembly. (30:4).

So they established a decree to circulate a proclamation throughout Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that the people should come to keep the Passover of the LORD, the God of Israel, in Jerusalem. For they had not observed it in great numbers as prescribed. (30:5).

At the command of the king, the couriers went throughout Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his officials, which read: “Children of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that He may return to those of you who remain, who have escaped the grasp of the kings of Assyria. (30:6).
Do not be like your fathers and brothers who were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of their fathers, so that He made them an object of horror, as you can see. (30:7).

Now do not stiffen your necks as your fathers did. Submit to the LORD and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever. Serve the LORD your God, so that His fierce anger will turn away from you. (30:8).

For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and sons will receive mercy in the presence of their captors and will return to this land. For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful; He will not turn His face away from you if you return to Him.” (30:9).
And the couriers traveled from city to city through the land of Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, but the people scorned and mocked them. (30:10).
Nevertheless, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. (30:11).
Moreover, the power of God was on the people in Judah to give them one heart to obey the command of the king and his officials according to the word of the LORD. (30:12).
In the second month, a very great assembly gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread. (30:13).
They proceeded to remove the altars in Jerusalem and to take away the incense altars and throw them into the Kidron Valley. (30:14).

And on the fourteenth day of the second month they slaughtered the Passover lamb. The priests and Levites were ashamed, and they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings to the house of the LORD. (30:15).
They stood at their prescribed posts, according to the Law of Moses the man of God. The priests splattered the blood, which they received from the hand of the Levites. (30:16).

Since there were many in the assembly who had not consecrated themselves, the Levites were in charge of slaughtering the Passover lambs for every unclean person to consecrate the lambs to the LORD. (30:17).

A large number of the people— many from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun— had not purified themselves, yet they ate the Passover, contrary to what was written. But Hezekiah interceded for them, saying, “May the LORD, who is good, provide atonement for everyone (30:18).
who sets his heart on seeking God — the LORD, the God of his fathers — even if he is not cleansed according to the purification rules of the sanctuary.” (30:19).
And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people. (30:20).

The Israelites who were present in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy, and the Levites and priests praised the LORD day after day, accompanied by loud instruments of praise to the LORD. (30:21).

And Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who performed skillfully before the LORD. For seven days they ate their assigned portion, sacrificing peace offerings and giving thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers. (30:22).
The whole assembly agreed to observe seven more days, so they observed seven days with joy. (30:23).

For Hezekiah king of Judah contributed a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for the assembly, and the officials contributed a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep for the assembly, and a great number of priests consecrated themselves. (30:24).

Then the whole assembly of Judah rejoiced along with the priests and Levites and the whole assembly that had come from Israel, including the foreigners who had come from Israel and those who lived in Judah. (30:25).
So there was great rejoicing in Jerusalem, for nothing like this had happened there since the days of Solomon son of David king of Israel. (30:26).
Then the priests and the Levites stood to bless the people, and God heard their voice, and their prayer came into His holy dwelling place in heaven. (30:27).
crossRefs: Numbers 9:6-13: Anyone unclean from a body or away on a journey keeps the Passover in the second month instead of the first.
Exodus 12:1-20: The Passover lamb in the first month, the blood on the doorposts, and seven days of unleavened bread.
Deuteronomy 16:1-8: Passover is to be sacrificed at the place the LORD chooses and not within your own towns.
2 Kings 23:21-23: No Passover like Josiah's had been kept since the days of the judges who judged Israel.
2 Chronicles 7:8-10: Solomon's assembly kept the feast seven days and seven more, the gathering this one is measured against.

translationNotes.note: The lamb was killed at dusk on the fourteenth day of the first month, its blood put on the doorframes the first time in Egypt, and the meat eaten that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs (Exodus 12:1-11). The name is the verb used when the LORD passed over the marked houses. It is one of the three feasts that required every man to come to the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 16:16), which is why keeping it turned into a national assembly.

Verses 2-3 move the feast a month late for two stated reasons: not enough priests had consecrated themselves, and the people were not gathered. The law already provided for exactly this. Numbers 9:6-13 allows a man who is unclean or away on a journey to keep Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month instead, and Hezekiah applies the provision to a whole nation.

Normally the head of each household killed his own Passover lamb (Exodus 12:3-6, 21). Verse 17 records the Levites doing the killing instead, for everyone in the crowd who had not purified himself. The change is procedural and the text gives the reason, and it is the arrangement Josiah's Passover uses again a century later (2 Chronicles 35:6,11).

Verse 6 sends runners with letters from the king through Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, territory that had been the northern kingdom until Assyria carried it off. There was no postal service; a royal message travelled on foot or by relay riders, and letters carried the king's seal as proof. Some towns laughed the runners out, and some came.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread runs seven days from the day after Passover (Leviticus 23:6). Verses 21-23 record the assembly keeping the seven days and then deciding to keep seven more, which doubles a fixed feast by common agreement. Solomon's dedication ran fourteen days the same way (2 Chronicles 7:8-9), and verse 26 says nothing like it had happened in Jerusalem since Solomon.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah to celebrate Passover in Jerusalem in the second month; despite ridicule and ceremonial irregularities, a large crowd gathers, removes idolatrous altars, and observes the festival for fourteen days with great rejoicing.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Chronicles 31
summaryBullets: When all this had ended, the Israelites in attendance went out to the cities of Judah and broke up the sacred pillars, chopped down the Asherah poles, and tore down the high places and altars throughout Judah and Benjamin, as well as in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had utterly destroyed them all. Then all the Israelites returned to their cities, each to his own property. (31:1).

Hezekiah reestablished the divisions of the priests and Levites — each of them according to their duties as priests or Levites — for the burnt offerings and peace offerings, for ministry, for giving thanks, and for singing praises at the gates of the LORD’s dwelling. (31:2).

The king contributed from his own possessions for the regular morning and evening burnt offerings and for the burnt offerings on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts, as written in the Law of the LORD. (31:3).
Moreover, he commanded the people living in Jerusalem to make a contribution for the priests and Levites so that they could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD. (31:4).

As soon as the order went out, the Israelites generously provided the firstfruits of the grain, new wine, oil, and honey, and of all the produce of the field, and they brought in an abundance — a tithe of everything. (31:5).

And the Israelites and Judahites who lived in the cities of Judah also brought a tithe of their herds and flocks and a tithe of the holy things consecrated to the LORD their God, and they laid them in large heaps. (31:6).
In the third month they began building up the heaps, and they finished in the seventh month. (31:7).
When Hezekiah and his officials came and viewed the heaps, they blessed the LORD and His people Israel. (31:8).
Then Hezekiah questioned the priests and Levites about the heaps, (31:9).

and Azariah, the chief priest of the household of Zadok, answered him, “Since the people began to bring their contributions into the house of the LORD, we have had enough to eat, and there is plenty left over, because the LORD has blessed His people; this great abundance is what is left over.” (31:10).
Then Hezekiah commanded them to prepare storerooms in the house of the LORD, and they did so. (31:11).
And they faithfully brought in the contributions, tithes, and dedicated gifts. Conaniah the Levite was the officer in charge of them, and his brother Shimei was second. (31:12).

Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were overseers under the authority of Conaniah and his brother Shimei, by appointment of King Hezekiah and of Azariah the chief official of the house of God. (31:13).
Kore son of Imnah the Levite, the keeper of the East Gate, was in charge of the freewill offerings given to God, distributing the contributions to the LORD and the consecrated gifts. (31:14).

Under his authority, Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah faithfully distributed portions to their fellow priests in their cities, according to their divisions, old and young alike. (31:15).

In addition, they distributed portions to the males registered by genealogy who were three years of age or older — to all who would enter the house of the LORD for their daily duties for service in the responsibilities of their divisions — (31:16).
and to the priests enrolled according to their families in the genealogy, as well as to the Levites twenty years of age or older, according to their responsibilities and divisions. (31:17).
The genealogy included all the little ones, wives, sons, and daughters of the whole assembly. For they had faithfully consecrated themselves as holy. (31:18).

As for the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who lived on the farmlands around each of their cities or in any other city, men were designated by name to distribute a portion to every male among the priests and to every Levite listed by the genealogies. (31:19).
So this is what Hezekiah did throughout Judah. He did what was good and upright and true before the LORD his God. (31:20).
He acted with all his heart in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law and the commandments, in order to seek his God. And so he prospered. (31:21).
crossRefs: Numbers 18:21-32: The tithe is given to the Levites for their service, and the Levites give a tenth of that tenth to the priests.
Leviticus 27:30-33: The tithe of the land, of seed and fruit and every tenth animal of herd and flock, is holy to the LORD.
Deuteronomy 14:22-29: The yearly tithe of grain, wine, and oil, and the third-year tithe stored in the towns for the Levite and the stranger.
Nehemiah 13:10-13: The Levites had gone back to their fields because their portions were not given, and Nehemiah restores the storerooms.
Malachi 3:8-10: Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house.

translationNotes.note: A tenth of the grain, wine, oil, and of the herds and flocks, brought in kind because there was no coinage to bring instead. Numbers 18:21-24 assigns it to the Levites in place of land, and Numbers 18:26 then requires the Levites to tithe a tenth of what they receive to the priests. Verses 5-6 record both the tithe and the firstfruits arriving together once Hezekiah reinstates the order.

The first portion of each harvest, brought to the sanctuary before any of that crop could be used (Exodus 23:19, Leviticus 23:9-14). It is a different obligation from the tithe: the tithe is a tenth of the whole, the firstfruits are the leading edge of the crop, and verse 5 lists them separately for grain, new wine, oil, and honey.

Verse 7 says the piles were begun in the third month and finished in the seventh. That is the whole agricultural year arriving in order: barley and wheat harvested in spring, then grapes, olives, and summer fruit through to autumn. The tithe came as produce, not money, so it had to be brought when each crop came in and stored where the priests lived.

Verse 11 has Hezekiah order chambers prepared in the house of the LORD, with a Levite in charge and a second under him. These side rooms along the temple were the granary and treasury of the whole system, and control of them was worth having: Nehemiah 13:4-9 finds one of them cleared out and given to Tobiah as a private apartment, and throws his furniture into the street.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִתְיַחֵשׂ (hityahes), to be enrolled by genealogy
translationNotes.note: Verses 16-19 describe a ration roll, not a census. Priests and Levites on duty drew a portion, and so did their households in the country towns, males from three years old up, with wives, sons, and daughters counted in. Payment came as food, so the registers had to record who was entitled, in which town, and by what descent.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israelites destroy pagan altars throughout the land, then Hezekiah organizes the priests and Levites by division and directs the people to support them with tithes and offerings; contributions pour in so abundantly from the third month through the seventh that storerooms must be built, with appointed Levites overseeing the distribution to priests and their families.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Chronicles 32
summaryBullets: After all these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah. He laid siege to the fortified cities, intending to conquer them for himself. (32:1).
When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come to make war against Jerusalem, (32:2).
he consulted with his leaders and mighty men about stopping up the waters of the springs outside the city, and they helped him carry it out. (32:3).
Many people assembled and stopped up all the springs and the stream that flowed through the land. “Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?” they said. (32:4).

Then Hezekiah worked resolutely to rebuild all the broken sections of the wall and to raise up towers on it. He also built an outer wall and reinforced the supporting terraces of the City of David, and he produced an abundance of weapons and shields. (32:5).
Hezekiah appointed military commanders over the people and gathered the people in the square of the city gate. Then he encouraged them, saying, (32:6).
“Be strong and courageous! Do not be afraid or discouraged before the king of Assyria and the vast army with him, for there is a greater One with us than with him. (32:7).
With him is only the arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God to help us and to fight our battles.” So the people were strengthened by the words of Hezekiah king of Judah. (32:8).

Later, as Sennacherib king of Assyria and all his forces besieged Lachish, he sent his servants to Jerusalem with a message for King Hezekiah of Judah and all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem: (32:9).
“This is what Sennacherib king of Assyria says: What is the basis of your confidence, that you remain in Jerusalem under siege? (32:10).
Is not Hezekiah misleading you to give you over to death by famine and thirst when he says, ‘The LORD our God will deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria ?’ (32:11).
Did not Hezekiah himself remove His high places and His altars and say to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before one altar, and on it you shall burn sacrifices’ ? (32:12).
Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of the lands? Have the gods of these nations ever been able to deliver their land from my hand? (32:13).
Who among all the gods of these nations that my fathers devoted to destruction has been able to deliver his people from my hand? How then can your God deliver you from my hand? (32:14).

So now, do not let Hezekiah deceive you, and do not let him mislead you like this. Do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to deliver his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you from my hand!” (32:15).
And the servants of Sennacherib spoke further against the LORD God and against His servant Hezekiah. (32:16).

He also wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel, and saying against Him: “Just as the gods of the nations did not deliver their people from my hand, so the God of Hezekiah will not deliver His people from my hand.” (32:17).
Then the Assyrians called out loudly in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten and terrify them in order to capture the city. (32:18).
They spoke against the God of Jerusalem as they had spoken against the gods of the peoples of the earth — the work of human hands. (32:19).
In response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz cried out to heaven in prayer, (32:20).

and the LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he withdrew to his own land in disgrace. And when he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons struck him down with the sword. (32:21).
So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from the hands of King Sennacherib of Assyria and all others, and He gave them rest on every side. (32:22).
Many brought offerings to Jerusalem for the LORD and valuable gifts for Hezekiah king of Judah, and from then on he was exalted in the eyes of all nations. (32:23).
In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. So he prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign. (32:24).
But because his heart was proud, Hezekiah did not repay the favor shown to him. Therefore wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem. (32:25).
Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart— he and the people of Jerusalem— so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah. (32:26).
Hezekiah had very great riches and honor, and he made treasuries for his silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all kinds of valuable articles. (32:27).
He also made storehouses for the harvest of grain and new wine and oil, stalls for all kinds of livestock, and pens for the flocks. (32:28).
He made cities for himself, and he acquired herds of sheep and cattle in abundance, for God gave him very great wealth. (32:29).
It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the Spring of Gihon and channeled it down to the west side of the City of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all that he did. (32:30).

And so when ambassadors of the rulers of Babylon were sent to him to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land, God left him alone to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart. (32:31).

As for the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his deeds of loving devotion, they are indeed written in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. (32:32).

And Hezekiah rested with his fathers and was buried in the upper tombs of David’s descendants. All Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor at his death. And his son Manasseh reigned in his place. (32:33).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18-20: Parallel account of Sennacherib, Hezekiah’s illness, and Babylonian envoys.
Isaiah 36-39: Prophetic account of the same events.
Joshua 1:9: 'Be strong and courageous' as encouragement in battle.
Psalm 46:1: 'God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.'
2 Chronicles 7:14: Humbling and prayer turn away wrath.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חִזְקוּ וְאִמְצוּ (ḥizqu v’emtzu), Greek: ἰσχύετε καὶ ἀνδρίζεσθε (ischyete kai andrizesthe), Aramaic: אתחזקו ואתאמצו (ethḥezequ v’eth’ametzu)
translationNotes.note: Covenant encouragement formula, used to call the people to trust in God rather than military strength.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּדֵּף (giddēf), Greek: βλασφημέω (blasphēmeō), Aramaic: גדף (gaddaf)
translationNotes.note: To mock, revile, or insult the name of God; a key element of Assyrian defiance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ (mal’akh), Greek: ἄγγελος (angelos), Aramaic: מַלְאָךְ (mal’akh)
translationNotes.note: Messenger or heavenly being. Here, an angel of the LORD brings sudden deliverance by striking down Assyria’s army.
Ambassadors sent from Babylon; their visit becomes a test of Hezekiah’s pride and loyalty.

Verse 30 says Hezekiah stopped the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channelled the water down to the west side of the city. The tunnel is still there: about 1,750 feet of rock cut under Jerusalem from the spring to the Pool of Siloam, driven by two teams working toward each other. An inscription found in it in 1880, now in Istanbul, records the moment the two crews heard each other's picks through the stone and broke through.

Verse 9 has Sennacherib besieging Lachish while he sends messengers to Jerusalem. Lachish was Judah's second city, guarding the approach to the hills from the southwest, about thirty miles from Jerusalem. Sennacherib carved the siege across a whole room of his palace at Nineveh, showing the ramp, the battering rams, and the people of Lachish led out; those panels are in the British Museum, and the ramp itself has been excavated at the site.

The threat in verse 11 and the boast in verses 13 to 15 sit on a known policy. Assyria did not usually garrison a conquered nation; it moved the population out and other conquered peoples in, breaking any base for revolt. Sargon II's annals claim 27,000 taken from Samaria in 722 BC, and Sennacherib's own account of this campaign claims 200,150 taken from Judah's towns.

stories.keyTakeaway: Sennacherib of Assyria invades, mocking God. Hezekiah strengthens the city and encourages the people to trust the LORD. Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and God sends an angel to destroy the Assyrian army. Hezekiah later becomes proud after healing and wealth, but humbles himself before death.

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Chronicles 33
summaryBullets: Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-five years. (33:1).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD by following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. (33:2).
For he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had torn down, and he raised up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles. And he worshiped and served all the host of heaven. (33:3).
Manasseh also built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, “My Name will remain in Jerusalem forever.” (33:4).
In both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven. (33:5).

He sacrificed his sons in the fire in the Valley of Ben-hinnom. He practiced sorcery, divination, and witchcraft, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did great evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger. (33:6).

Manasseh even took the carved image he had made and set it up in the house of God, of which God had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this temple and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will establish My Name forever. (33:7).

I will never again cause the feet of the Israelites to leave the land that I assigned to your fathers, if only they are careful to do all that I have commanded them through Moses— all the laws, statutes, and judgments.” (33:8).
So Manasseh led the people of Judah and Jerusalem astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. (33:9).
And the LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen. (33:10).
So the LORD brought against them the military commanders of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh, put a hook in his nose, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon. (33:11).
And in his distress, Manasseh sought the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbled himself before the God of his fathers. (33:12).
And when he prayed to Him, the LORD received his plea and heard his petition. So He brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God. (33:13).

After this, Manasseh rebuilt the outer wall of the City of David from west of Gihon in the valley to the entrance of the Fish Gate, and he brought it around the hill of Ophel and heightened it considerably. He also stationed military commanders in all the fortified cities of Judah. (33:14).
He removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, along with all the altars he had built on the temple mount and in Jerusalem, and he dumped them outside the city. (33:15).
Then he restored the altar of the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings and thank offerings on it, and he told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. (33:16).
Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God. (33:17).

As for the rest of the acts of Manasseh, along with his prayer to his God and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, they are indeed written in the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (33:18).

His prayer and how God received his plea, as well as all his sin and unfaithfulness, and the sites where he built high places and set up Asherah poles and idols before he humbled himself, they are indeed written in the Records of the Seers. (33:19).
And Manasseh rested with his fathers and was buried at his palace. And his son Amon reigned in his place. (33:20).
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem two years. (33:21).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh had done. Amon served and sacrificed to all the idols that his father Manasseh had made, (33:22).
but he did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done; instead, Amon increased his guilt. (33:23).
Then the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed him in his palace. (33:24).
But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place. (33:25).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 21:1-26: Parallel account of Manasseh and Amon.
Deuteronomy 4:25-27: Warning that idolatry leads to exile among the nations.
1 Kings 8:46-50: Solomon’s prayer: if exiled, repent and pray toward this house, God will hear.
Isaiah 55:6-7: Call to seek the LORD and turn from wickedness.
Prayer of Manasseh 1: A penitential prayer attributed to Manasseh in exile, arising from the account in this chapter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֹחִים (ḥochim), Greek: ἄγκιστρα (ankistra), Aramaic: חוחין (ḥochin)
translationNotes.note: Used to lead captives by the nose or jaw; symbol of humiliation in Assyrian practice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּנַע (kanaʿ), Greek: ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), Aramaic: כנע (knaʿ)
translationNotes.note: To bow down, submit. Manasseh deeply abases himself before God in repentance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּמָה (bamah), Greek: βωμός (bōmos), Aramaic: במתא (bamatha)
translationNotes.note: Elevated worship sites; often condemned when linked to idolatry, though sometimes used for the LORD.
A penitential prayer preserved in Greek tradition, included in some canons as a model of repentance.

translationNotes.term: The carved image in the house of God
translationNotes.note: Verses 3 and 7 have Manasseh set up altars to Baal, make Asherah poles, and put a carved image inside the temple itself. Asherah was worshipped as a mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or living tree set beside an altar, which is why the reforming kings are always described cutting them down and burning them. Putting one in the house God had named as His own is the specific charge in verse 7.

Verse 6 lists soothsaying, omen reading, sorcery, mediums, and necromancers together. These were paid professionals in the ancient world: readers of livers and entrails, interpreters of bird flight and dreams, and specialists who claimed to call up the dead for a fee. Deuteronomy 18:9-14 forbids the whole list, and Saul's night at Endor shows a king breaking his own ban to use one (1 Samuel 28:3-19).

Verse 11 has Assyrian commanders take Manasseh to Babylon with hooks and bronze fetters. Assyrian royal inscriptions name him twice from their own side: Esarhaddon, who reigned 681 to 669 BC, lists Manasseh king of Judah among twenty-two vassal kings ordered to haul building timber and stone to Nineveh, and Ashurbanipal lists him again among kings supplying troops for the Egyptian campaign.

stories.keyTakeaway: Manasseh plunges Judah into idolatry, is taken captive to Babylon, but humbles himself and is restored, removing idols and repairing the altar. His son Amon reigns briefly in evil, refuses humility, and is killed by his servants.

stories.title: 📖 2 Chronicles 34
summaryBullets: Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years. (34:1).
And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father David; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left. (34:2).

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, Josiah began to seek the God of his father David, and in the twelfth year he began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images. (34:3).

Then in his presence the altars of the Baals were torn down, and he cut to pieces the incense altars that were above them. He shattered the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images, crushed them to dust, and scattered them over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. (34:4).
Then he burned the bones of the priests on their altars. So he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem. (34:5).
Josiah did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, and in the ruins around them. (34:6).
He tore down the altars and Asherah poles, crushed the idols to powder, and cut to pieces all the incense altars throughout the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem. (34:7).

Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, in order to cleanse the land and the temple, Josiah sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God. (34:8).

So they went to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that had been brought into the house of God, which the Levites who guarded the doors had collected from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the remnant of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the people of Jerusalem. (34:9).
They put it into the hands of those supervising the work in the house of the LORD, who in turn gave it to the workmen restoring and repairing the house of the LORD. (34:10).
They also gave money to the carpenters and builders to buy dressed stone, as well as timbers for couplings and beams for the buildings that the kings of Judah had allowed to deteriorate. (34:11).

And the men did the work faithfully. The Levites overseeing them were Jahath and Obadiah, descendants of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, descendants of Kohath. Other Levites, all skilled with musical instruments, (34:12).
were over the laborers and supervised all who did the work, task by task. Some of the Levites were secretaries, officers, and gatekeepers. (34:13).
While they were bringing out the money that had been taken into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given by Moses. (34:14).
And Hilkiah said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!” And he gave it to Shaphan. (34:15).
Then Shaphan brought the book to the king and reported, “Your servants are doing all that has been placed in their hands. (34:16).
They have paid out the money that was found in the house of the LORD and have put it into the hands of the supervisors and workers.” (34:17).
Moreover , Shaphan the scribe told the king, “Hilkiah the priest has given me a book.” And Shaphan read it in the presence of the king. (34:18).
When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes (34:19).
and commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the servant of the king: (34:20).

“Go and inquire of the LORD for me and for those remaining in Israel and Judah concerning the words in the book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that has been poured out on us because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD by doing all that is written in this book.” (34:21).

So Hilkiah and those the king had designated went and spoke to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, the son of Hasrah, the keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem, in the Second District. (34:22).
And Huldah said to them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Tell the man who sent you (34:23).

that this is what the LORD says: I am about to bring calamity on this place and on its people, according to all the curses written in the book that has been read in the presence of the king of Judah, (34:24).

because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods, that they might provoke Me to anger with all the works of their hands. My wrath will be poured out upon this place and will not be quenched.’ (34:25).
But as for the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘As for the words that you heard, (34:26).

because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard His words against this place and against its people, and because you have humbled yourself before Me and have torn your clothes and wept before Me, I have heard you,’ declares the LORD. (34:27).

‘Now I will indeed gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place and on its people.’” So they brought her answer back to the king. (34:28).
Then the king summoned all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. (34:29).

And he went up to the house of the LORD with all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, as well as the priests and the Levites— all the people great and small— and in their hearing he read all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. (34:30).

So the king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, decrees, and statutes with all his heart and all his soul, and to carry out the words of the covenant that were written in this book. (34:31).
Then he had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin take a stand in agreement to it. So all the people of Jerusalem carried out the covenant of God, the God of their fathers. (34:32).

And Josiah removed all the abominations from all the lands belonging to the Israelites, and he required everyone in Israel to serve the LORD their God. Throughout his reign they did not turn aside from following the LORD, the God of their fathers. (34:33).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 22:1-20: The same repair of the temple, the same book found by Hilkiah, and the same word from Huldah.
1 Kings 13:1-2: A man of God cries out against the altar at Bethel and names Josiah generations before he is born.
Deuteronomy 31:24-26: Moses puts the book of the law beside the ark of the covenant as a witness against Israel.
Deuteronomy 28:15-68: The curses read out for breaking the covenant, the words that make Josiah tear his clothes.
2 Kings 23:15-20: Josiah pulls down the altar at Bethel and burns the bones out of the tombs on it, as the man of God had said.

translationNotes.note: A book at this period is a scroll of sheets sewn end to end, written on leather or papyrus and rolled, not a bound volume. Verse 15 has Hilkiah find one in the temple during the repairs and hand it to the royal secretary, who reads it aloud to the king; there was no expectation that the king read it himself. Deuteronomy 31:24-26 has Moses order the book of the law placed beside the ark, and 17:18-19 requires each king to have a copy made and read it all his life.

Verse 19 records the king's reaction to hearing the book read. Tearing the garment from the neck down was the standard public sign of grief or horror in Israel, used at news of a death (Genesis 37:34), at defeat, and at blasphemy heard in court (Matthew 26:65). It was a visible act done in front of witnesses, which is why the text records who saw it.

Verse 5 has Josiah burn the bones of the pagan priests on their own altars. Contact with a human corpse or grave made a person or place unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), so scattering the dust of the idols over the graves of their worshippers and burning bones on the altars put those sites permanently out of use. 2 Kings 23:15-18 records him doing the same at Bethel.

Shaphan in verses 8-18 is not a copyist. The sofer was a cabinet officer of the crown, listed with the army commander and the recorder among the king's chief men (2 Samuel 8:16-17), handling correspondence, records, and revenue; 2 Kings 12:10 has the king's secretary count the temple money alongside the high priest. Verse 8 sends him out with the governor of the city and the recorder, mazkir, another standing office of state.

Verse 22 sends the high priest, the king's secretary, and three other senior officials to a woman living in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem to authenticate the book. Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both prophesying at the time, and the delegation went to Huldah. She is one of a small number of women named as prophets in Scripture, with Miriam, Deborah, and Noadiah (Exodus 15:20, Judges 4:4, Nehemiah 6:14).

stories.keyTakeaway: Josiah becomes king at eight, spends his youth destroying idols and high places throughout Judah and Israel, and at eighteen sends officials to repair the temple; during repairs Hilkiah discovers the Book of the Law, which Josiah reads and tears his robes in distress. The prophet Huldah tells Josiah disaster will come on Judah but he will die in peace for his repentant heart, so Josiah gathers all the people and renews the covenant to follow the LORD.

headings.text: Hilkiah Finds the Book of the Law

stories.title: 📖 2 Chronicles 35
summaryBullets: Then Josiah kept the Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem, and the Passover lamb was slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month. (35:1).
He appointed the priests to their duties and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD. (35:2).

To the Levites who taught all Israel and were holy to the LORD, Josiah said: “Put the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon son of David king of Israel. It is not to be carried around on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and His people Israel. (35:3).
Prepare yourselves by families in your divisions, according to the instructions written by David king of Israel and Solomon his son. (35:4).
Moreover, stand in the Holy Place by the divisions of the families of your kinsmen the lay people, and by the divisions of the families of the Levites. (35:5).
Slaughter the Passover lambs, consecrate yourselves, and make preparations for your fellow countrymen to carry out the word of the LORD given by Moses.” (35:6).
From his own flocks and herds Josiah contributed 30,000 lambs and goats plus 3,000 bulls for the Passover offerings for all the people who were present. (35:7).

His officials also contributed willingly to the people and priests and Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officials of the house of God, gave the priests 2,600 Passover offerings and 300 bulls. (35:8).

Additionally, Conaniah and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, as well as Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, officers of the Levites, contributed to the Levites 5,000 Passover offerings and 500 bulls. (35:9).
So the service was prepared; the priests stood in their places and the Levites in their divisions according to the king’s command. (35:10).
And they slaughtered the Passover lambs, while the priests splattered the blood handed to them and the Levites skinned the animals. (35:11).

They set aside the burnt offerings to be given to the divisions of the families of the people to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the Book of Moses. And they did the same with the bulls. (35:12).
They roasted the Passover animals on the fire according to the regulation, and they boiled the other holy offerings in pots, kettles, and bowls and quickly brought them to all the people. (35:13).

Afterward, they made preparations for themselves and for the priests, since the priests, the descendants of Aaron, were offering up burnt offerings and fat until nightfall. So the Levites made preparations for themselves and for the priests, the descendants of Aaron. (35:14).

The singers, the descendants of Asaph, were at their stations according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king’s seer. And the gatekeepers at each gate did not need to leave their posts, because their fellow Levites made preparations for them. (35:15).
So on that day the entire service of the LORD was carried out for celebrating the Passover and offering burnt offerings on the altar of the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah. (35:16).
The Israelites who were present also observed the Passover at that time, as well as the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days. (35:17).

No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel ever observed a Passover like the one that Josiah observed with the priests, the Levites, all Judah, the Israelites who were present, and the people of Jerusalem. (35:18).
In the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign, this Passover was observed. (35:19).
After all this, when Josiah had set the temple in order, Neco king of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish by the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to confront him. (35:20).

But Neco sent messengers to him, saying, “What is the issue between you and me, O king of Judah? I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another dynasty, and God has told me to hurry. So stop opposing God, who is with me, or He will destroy you!” (35:21).

Josiah, however, did not turn away from him; instead, in order to engage him in battle, he disguised himself. He did not listen to Neco’s words from the mouth of God, but went to fight him on the Plain of Megiddo. (35:22).
There the archers shot King Josiah, who said to his servants, “Take me away, for I am badly wounded!” (35:23).

So his servants took him out of his chariot, put him in his second chariot, and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died. And Josiah was buried in the tomb of his fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him. (35:24).

Then Jeremiah lamented over Josiah, and to this day all the male and female singers recite laments over Josiah. They established them as a statute for Israel, and indeed they are written in the Book of Laments. (35:25).
As for the rest of the acts of Josiah and his deeds of loving devotion according to what is written in the Law of the LORD— (35:26).
his acts from beginning to end— they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. (35:27).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 23:21-30: The same Passover kept at Jerusalem, and Josiah's death when he goes out against Pharaoh Neco.
Exodus 12:1-11: The Passover lamb roasted with fire and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, with belts fastened and staff in hand.
Deuteronomy 16:5-7: The Passover may not be sacrificed within your towns, but only at the place the LORD chooses.
Jeremiah 46:2: The word against Pharaoh Neco's army at Carchemish by the Euphrates, defeated in Jehoiakim's fourth year.
Zechariah 12:11: The mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo.

translationNotes.note: Verse 3 has Josiah tell the Levites to put the holy ark in the house and stop carrying it on their shoulders. Carrying it was their inherited job (Numbers 4:15, 1 Chronicles 15:15), and the order means the ark had been out of the Most Holy Place, most likely moved during the reigns that filled the temple with other worship. This is the last time Scripture records the ark being handled.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּשַׁל (bashal), to cook or boil - צָלָה (tsalah), to roast
translationNotes.note: Verse 13 says they roasted the Passover animals on the fire as prescribed and boiled the other holy offerings in pots, kettles, and bowls. Exodus 12:8-9 requires the Passover lamb roasted and forbids it boiled in water. Deuteronomy 16:7 uses bashal, the general word for cooking, which the older passage restricts to roasting; this verse keeps the two operations separate and names which food gets which.

Verses 7-9 record the animals provided: 30,000 lambs and goats and 3,000 bulls from the king's own flocks, with thousands more from the officials, because every household attending needed a lamb (Exodus 12:3). Verse 18 says no Passover like it had been kept since Samuel's day. This is the last one recorded before Jerusalem falls.

A fortified mound guarding the narrow Aruna pass where the international coast road cuts through the Carmel ridge into the Jezreel Valley. Any army moving between Egypt and Mesopotamia had to come through it, which is why the site has been fought over from Thutmose III onward and why Josiah went out to stop Neco there in verse 22. The Greek form of its name, Har Megiddo, is the Armageddon of Revelation 16:16.

Neco II of Egypt, who reigned 610 to 595 BC. Verse 21 has him say he is not marching against Judah at all; he was going north to prop up the last of Assyria against Babylon at Carchemish on the Euphrates. Babylonian chronicle tablets record that campaign and Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of the Egyptian army there in 605 BC.

A qinah is a funeral song with its own limping rhythm, a long line answered by a short one, the shape of the whole book of Lamentations. Verse 25 says Jeremiah made one for Josiah, that the singers kept reciting them long after, and that they were written in a collection called the Book of Laments. That collection does not survive and is not the biblical book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of Jerusalem.

stories.keyTakeaway: Josiah organizes an elaborate Passover celebration in Jerusalem with priests, Levites, and officials contributing thousands of animals; the festival is observed more magnificently than any since the prophet Samuel's time. After the Passover, Josiah engages King Necho of Egypt in battle at Megiddo against Necho's warning, is wounded by archers, and dies in Jerusalem.

stories.title: 📜 2 Chronicles 36
summaryBullets: Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father. (36:1).
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. (36:2).
And the king of Egypt dethroned him in Jerusalem and imposed on Judah a levy of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. (36:3).

Then Neco king of Egypt made Eliakim brother of Jehoahaz king over Judah and Jerusalem, and he changed Eliakim’s name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Eliakim’s brother Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt. (36:4).
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. And he did evil in the sight of the LORD his God. (36:5).
Then Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jehoiakim and bound him with bronze shackles to take him to Babylon. (36:6).
Nebuchadnezzar also took to Babylon some of the articles from the house of the LORD, and he put them in his temple in Babylon. (36:7).

As for the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, the abominations he committed, and all that was found against him, they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. And his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place. (36:8).
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months and ten days. And he did evil in the sight of the LORD. (36:9).

In the spring, King Nebuchadnezzar summoned Jehoiachin and brought him to Babylon, along with the articles of value from the house of the LORD. And he made Jehoiachin’s relative Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem. (36:10).
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. (36:11).
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD his God and did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke for the LORD. (36:12).
He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. But Zedekiah stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel. (36:13).

Furthermore, all the leaders of the priests and the people multiplied their unfaithful deeds, following all the abominations of the nations, and they defiled the house of the LORD, which He had consecrated in Jerusalem. (36:14).
Again and again the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent word to His people through His messengers because He had compassion on them and on His dwelling place. (36:15).
But they mocked the messengers of God, despising His words and scoffing at His prophets, until the wrath of the LORD against His people was stirred up beyond remedy. (36:16).

So He brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who put their young men to the sword in the sanctuary, sparing neither young men nor young women, neither elderly nor infirm. God gave them all into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, (36:17).
who carried off everything to Babylon— all the articles of the house of God, both large and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the king and his officials. (36:18).
Then the Chaldeans set fire to the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem. They burned down all the palaces and destroyed every article of value. (36:19).
Those who escaped the sword were carried by Nebuchadnezzar into exile in Babylon, and they became servants to him and his sons until the kingdom of Persia came to power. (36:20).
So the land enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation, until seventy years were completed, in fulfillment of the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah. (36:21).

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows: (36:22).

“This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to His people, may the LORD his God be with him, and may he go up.’” (36:23).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 25:11-12: Seventy years of Babylonian exile foretold.
Jeremiah 29:10: Promise of return after seventy years.
2 Kings 24-25: Parallel account of Judah’s fall and exile.
Daniel 1:1-2: Exile of Jehoiakim and temple vessels.
Ezra 1:1-4: Cyrus’s decree repeated, beginning restoration.
Isaiah 44:28-45:1: Cyrus prophesied as God’s shepherd and anointed.

translationNotes.note: Means 'The LORD has grasped.' Reigned briefly before being deposed by Egypt.
Means 'The LORD raises up.' Reigned wickedly, plundered by Babylon.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוֹיָכִין (Yeho-yakhin), Greek: Ιεχονιας (Iechonias), Aramaic: יכניה (Yekonya)
translationNotes.note: Also called Coniah. Means 'The LORD establishes.' Taken captive at a young age.
Means 'The LORD is righteousness.' He rebelled against Babylon and hardened against God’s word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵין מַרְפֵּא (ʾein marpe); Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν ἴασις (ouk estin iasis)
translationNotes.note: Indicates incurable condition; Judah’s sin reached the point where judgment was inevitable.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוֹרֶשׁ (Koresh), Greek: Κυρος (Kyros), Aramaic: כורש (Koresh)
translationNotes.note: Persian king who conquered Babylon and issued decree for Jewish return; called God’s 'shepherd' in Isaiah.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

About 75 lbs (34 kg) of metal. A 'talent of gold' in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Samuel 12:30) refers to physical mass rather than coined currency. The bronze for the Tabernacle (Exodus 38:29) was 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

intro:
2 Chronicles does not name its author. Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Baba Bathra 15a) attributes the book to Ezra the priest and scribe, continuing the literary project begun in 1 Chronicles and drawing on the same sources: official court records, royal annals, and earlier prophetic histories. The book reached its final form in post-exilic Jerusalem around 450-430 BC, during or shortly after Ezra's reform of the returned community. The same Ezra who later wrote the book of Ezra; 2 Chronicles closes with Cyrus's decree of 538 BC (36:22-23), and Ezra opens with the same decree (1:1-3), the textual marker that Jewish tradition cites as the link between the two books as a single literary project from Ezra's hand. Tradition also holds that Nehemiah completed the final genealogies of Chronicles after Ezra's death. Ezra was a priest of the line of Aaron through Phinehas (Ezra 7:1-5), a "skilled scribe in the Law of Moses" (Ezra 7:6), sent from Babylon to Jerusalem in 458 BC by the Persian king Artaxerxes I with royal authority to teach the Law and reorganize the temple worship. The events of 2 Chronicles cover roughly 970 to 538 BC, beginning with Solomon's accession after David's death, continuing through the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam (931 BC), the dynasty of David in Judah through the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem (586 BC) and the seventy-year exile, and closing with Cyrus's decree (538 BC) permitting the return. The historical setting of the writing is the Persian period under the Achaemenid Empire; the second temple had been completed in 516 BC under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest, with the encouragement of Haggai and Zechariah; the returned community was small, poor, and surrounded by hostile neighbors (Samaritans to the north, Ammonites and Edomites to the south and east). Persia's emperors Cyrus the Great, Darius I, Xerxes I (Ahasuerus of Esther), and Artaxerxes I each played roles in the restoration. Egypt was a Persian satrapy under the 27th Dynasty; Greece was beginning its Classical period with Athens at its height under Pericles.

2 Chronicles and 1 Chronicles were originally a single Hebrew book called Divrei HaYamim ("Events of the Days" or "Words of the Days"), divided by the Greek Septuagint translators (3rd century BC) into two and renamed Paraleipomena ("Things Omitted"). The Latin Vulgate adopted the Greek division but renamed it Chronica ("Chronicles") at Jerome's suggestion, and English Bibles inherited that title. In the Jewish canon, Chronicles is the closing book of the Ketuvim (Writings) and thus the final book of the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Chronicles were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the Persian period or shortly after.
